docs.title: Convexity
docs.text:
Optimization problems are frequently of the form:

\[ \min_{x \in \Omega} f(x) \text{ s.t. } g(x) \geq 0 \]

where \(f(x)\) is a loss function subject to (optional) constraint \(g(x) \geq 0\). \(f(x)\) is convex, \(\Omega\) is some convex set and \(g(x)\) is a convex function.

For example, regression tasks can be framed as follows: for \(y \in \R\), find \(f: X \to \R\) s.t. \(f = \argmin_f \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2\).

It is possible to take discrete, intractable problems to continuous space and optimize them there.

Definition 1.1.1: Convex Set

\(\Omega\) denotes a convex set if \(\forall x, y \in \Omega\) and for any \(t \in [0, 1], tx + (1 - t)y \in \Omega\). The line between two points in a convex set must also exist entirely in the convex set.

Definition 1.1.2: Convex Function

\(f: \Omega \to \R\) is a convex function iff \(\Omega\) is a convex set and \(\forall x, y \in \Omega\) where \(t \in [0, 1]\), \(f(tx + (1 - t)y) \leq tf(x) + (1 - t) f(y)\). Every point on the interpolation passed through \(f\) lies below or on the interpolation of the end-points passed through \(f\).

Equivalent characterizations - the function between two end-points lies beneath the secant line or the epigraph (set of points above the function) is a convex set.

Definition 1.1.3: Local Minima

\(\omega \in \Omega\) is a local minimum for convex function \(f\) if \(\forall u, ||\omega - u|| \leq \rho\) and \(f(u) \geq f(\omega)\). Here, \(\rho\) is a small threshold distance which defines a region around \(\omega\). \(u\) represents the set of points in the convex domain which fall inside that region.

Proposition 1.1.4: Every Local Minima is a Global Minima for a Convex Function

Suppose \(f\) is convex and \(\omega^*\) is a local minima. Then, \(\omega^*\) is a global minima for \(f\).

Proof

Let \(\omega_0\) be the global minima such that \(f(\omega_0) < f(\omega^*)\). By convexity of \(f\), we have that:

\[ f(t \omega_0 + (1 - t) \omega^*) \leq t f(\omega_0) + (1 - t) f(\omega^*) \]

Since \(f(\omega_0) < f(\omega^*)\),

\[ t f(\omega_0) + (1 - t) f(\omega^*) < t f(\omega^*) + (1 - t) f(\omega^*) = f(\omega^*) \]

Since \(\omega^*\) is a local minimum, there exists some region where \(f(\omega^*) \leq f(u)\) for all \(u\) where \(||\omega^* - u || \leq \rho\). However, we also know that \(f(t \omega_0 + (1 - t) \omega^*) \leq f(\omega^*)\).

This is a contradiction. With a sufficiently high \(t\), the point \(u(t) = t \omega_0 + (1 - t) \omega^*\) can get arbitrarily close to \(\omega^*\) meaning that for any \(\rho\), we can find \(t\) where \(||\omega^* - u(t)|| \leq \rho\). By convexity, we know that \(f(u(t)) < f(\omega^*)\). However, by the definition of local-minima, we know that \(f(u(t)) \geq f(\omega^*)\). Therefore, the assumption that there must exist some \(\omega_0\) where \(f(\omega_0) < f(\omega^*)\) is false. The local minimum of a convex function must also be a global minimum.

Intuitively, there can be no purely local minima in a convex function. In order for a point to be in a local minima, it must be surrounded by some kind of valley. We could draw a chord between the local and global minima and the walls of the valley would exist above the chord violating the convexity assumption. This chord is called the secant line.

Proposition 1.1.5: First Order Conditions for Local Minima

  • \(x\) is a local minima iff \(\nabla f(x) = 0\) and there are no other constraints. This is a necessary and sufficient condition for local minima under the assumption that \(f(x)\) is convex. If \(f(x)\) isn't convex, this is just a necessary condition.
  • \(x\) is a local minima if for all \(y \in \Omega\), \(\nabla f(y)^T (y - x) \geq 0\). Moving from \(x\) to any other feasible point does not decrease the value of the function.

The second condition - pick any point. Look at the gradient of \(f\) evaluated at that point and the difference vector with the local minima. The two will point in the same direction.

docs.title: Convex Sets
docs.text:
Recall that we say a set is convex if the line segment between any two points \(x, y \in \Omega\) lies within \(\Omega\).

In the right set, you can draw a chord which goes outside the set so the set is not convex.

Formally, \(\Omega\) is convex if \(\forall x, y \in \Omega\) and for any \(t \in [0, 1], tx + (1 - t)y \in \Omega\).

Definition 1.2.1: Convex Hull

The convex hull is the set of all convex combinations of points in a set \(C\).

\[ \text{conv } C = \left \{ a_1 x_1 + \dots + a_k x_k \mid x_i \in C, a_i \geq 0, \sum_{i = 1}^k a_i = 1 \right \} \]

Naturally, the convex hull is always convex and it is the smallest convex set that contains \(C\).

We list examples of convex sets.

Example 1.2.1: Convex Sets

  • The \(l_2\)-Ball. Formally, \(B(r) = \{x: ||x||_2 \leq r\}\).

  • The Half-space in \(d = 2\). \(\{Ax + b \leq 0\} \in \R^d\).

  • The Simplex. \(\Delta = \{P \mid P \geq 0, \sum_{i = 1}^d P_i = 1\}\).

Convexity is preserved under intersection. If \(S_1, S_2\) are convex then \(S_1 \cap S_2\) is convex.

Affine functions preserve convexity. \(C = A \Omega + b\).

Linear fractions preserve convexity.

Unions however do not preserve convexity.

docs.title: Convexity Conditions
docs.text:
Theorem 1.3.1: First Order Conditions

Recall that \(f\) is convex iff \( orall x, y \in \Omega\),

\[ f(x) \geq f(y) + abla f(y)^T (x - y) \]

\(f(x) \geq f(y) + abla f(y)^T (x - y)\) is just saying that a convex function is bounded below by its tangent line (while it is bounded above by its secant line) as the RHS is the first-order Taylor approximation of \(f\) around \(y\) evaluated at \(x\).

Proof

Suppose \(x_0 = tx + (1 - t)y\). We know that \(f(x) \geq f(x_0) + abla f(x_0)^T (x - x_0)\) and \(f(y) \geq f(x_0) + abla f(x_0)^T (y - x_0)\). WTS \(f\) is convex.

Then (the following three equations are independent),

\[ t f(x) + (1 - t) f(y) \geq t (f(x_0) + abla f(x_0)^T (x - x_0)) + (1 - t) (f(x_0) + abla f(x_0)^T (y - x_0)) \] \[ t f(x_0) + (1 - t) f(x_0) = f(x_0) \] \[ t(x - x_0) + (1 - t)(y - x_0) = tx + (1 - t)y - x_0 \]

However, note that \(x_0 = tx + (1 - t)y\) so the vector being multiplied against the inner-product is \(0\). Therefore,

\[ t f(x) + (1 - t) f(y) \geq f(tx + (1 - t)y) \]

Therefore, \(f\) is convex.

Next, we prove the other direction. Suppose that \(f(tx + (1 - t)y) \leq t f(x) + (1 - t) f(y)\). WTS that \(f(x) \geq f(y) + abla f(y)^T (x - y)\).

Then,

\[ rac{f(tx + (1 - t)y)}{t} \leq f(x) - f(y) + rac{f(y)}{t} \] \[ f(x) \geq f(y) + rac{f(tx + (1 - t)y) - f(y)}{t} \]

In the limit as \(t o 0\), this becomes:

\[ f(x) \geq f(y) + abla f(y)^T(x - y) \]

Theorem 1.3.2: Second Order Condition

Given \(\Omega \in \R^d\), \(f\) is convex iff \( orall x \in \Omega\),

\[ abla^2 f(x) \geq 0 \]

or for all \(h \in \R^d, x \in \Omega\),

\[ h^T abla^2 f(x) h \geq 0 \]

where \( abla^2 f\) is the Hessian of \(f\).

Proof

Suppose \( abla f(x)\) is PSD. Then, Taylor's approximation yields

\[ f(x + h) \approx f(x) + h^T abla f(x) + rac{1}{2} h^T abla^2 f(x) h \]

Since \( abla^2 f(x)\) is PSD, it follows that the last term is larger than \(0\). So:

\[ f(x + h) \geq f(x) + h^T abla f(x) \]

docs.title: Jensen's Inequality
docs.text:
Jensen's Inequality is an incredibly useful inequality.

Definition 1.3.3: Jensen's Inequality

Let \(f\) be convex. Then,

\[ f(\E_p[x]) \leq \E_p[f(x)] \]

If \(f\) is linear, clearly, the two would be identical. However, since \(f\) is convex, it pulls upwards meaning that the average of the outputs is greater than the output of the average.

Proof

Jensen's inequality is the generalization of convexity to convex combinations. We proceed via induction.

The base case is simply the definition of convexity.

Now suppose Jensen's inequality holds for \(n - 1\) points. Then,

\[ p_1 x_1 + \dots + p_n x_n = p_n x_n + (1 - p_n) \hat{x} \]

where \(\hat{x} = \sum_{i = 1}^{n - 1} \frac{p_i}{1 - p_n} x_i\). By convexity,

\[ f(p_n x_n + (1 - p_n) \hat{x}) \leq p_n f(x_n) + (1 - p_n) f(\hat{x}) \]

Now, we can apply our induction hypothesis to \(f(\hat{x})\).

\[ f(\hat{x}) \leq \sum_{i = 1}^{n - 1} \frac{p_i}{1 - p_n} f(x_i) \]

Therefore,

\[ f(\sum_{i = 1}^n p_i x_i) \leq \sum_{i = 1}^n p_i f(x_i) \]

docs.title: Convex Functions
docs.text:
1. Affine Functions, \(f(x) = a^T x + b\) can be shown to be convex using the second-order condition.

  2. Quadratic functions, \(f(x) = x^T Q x + b^T x + c\) where \(Q\) is symmetric PSD. Can also be shown to be convex using the 2nd order condition.

  3. Vector norms, $\(||x||_p = \left ( \sum_{i = 1}^d |x_i|^p \right )^{1/p}\) where \(p \geq 1\). Proof is given below.

  4. \(\text{Tr}(Ax)\) where \(A \in \R^{p \times d}, x \in \R^{d \times p}\). This is convex since the trace is a linear function.

  5. Matrix norms: \(||x||_{\text{op}} = \lambda_{\text{max}}(x)\).

  6. Frobenius Norm: \(||A||_F = \sqrt{\text{Tr}(A^T A)}\).

  7. LogSumExp: \(f(x) = \log \sum_{i = 0}^n \exp(x_i)\).

We prove vector norms are convex.

Proof

By the triangle inequality and zeroth order convexity condition (definition of convexity),

\[ ||tx + (1 - t)y||_p \leq ||tx||_p + ||(1 - t)y||_p = t ||x||_p + (1 - t) ||y||_p \]

Therefore,

\[ ||tx + (1 - t)y||_p \leq t ||x||_p + (1 - t) ||y||_p \]

We prove that LogSumExp is convex.

Proof

\[ \nabla f(x) = \left [ \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{i = 1}^n \exp(x_i)} \right ] \]

The gradient is a probability distribution. Let \(p_i = \nabla f(x_i)\). Then, use the quotient rule to find that:

\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_i} = p_i - p_i^2 \] \[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j \partial x_i} = - p_i p_j \]

Element-wise, \(H(f(x)) = \text{diag}(p) - pp^T\).

This is a covariance matrix of a one-hot vector that equals \(e_i\) with probability \(p_i\). Covariance matrices are PSD so \(f(x)\) is convex.

docs.title: Convexity Preserving Operations
docs.text:
1. Non-negative weighted sum of convex functions: \(f(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \alpha_i f_i(x)\) where \(\alpha_i \geq 0, f_i\) is convex.

  2. Letting \(n \to \infty\) and \(\sum_i \alpha_i = 1\), this becomes an expectation function, \(g(x) = \E_{\alpha}[f(x_i)]\).

  3. The max operation is convex.

  4. Composite functions. \(g(x) = f(h(x))\). If \(f\) is convex, strictly increasing and \(h\) is convex, then \(g\) is convex. If \(f\) is convex, strictly decreasing and \(h\) is concave, then \(g(x)\) is convex.

As an application, we derive the variational lower-bound for maximum likelihood estimation.

docs.title: Variational Lower Bound
docs.text:
Suppose \(p(x, z) = p(x \mid z) p(z)\). We wantn to use MLE to maximize \(\log p(x)\).

\[ L(z) = - \sum_{i = 1}^n \log p(x) \] \[ = - \sum_{i = 1}^n \log \int_z p(x, y) dz \] \[ = - \sum_{i = 1}^n \log \int_z \frac{p(x_i, z)}{q(z \mid x_i)} q(z \mid x_i) dz \]

A log function is concave so negative log is convex. By Jensen's inequality, we know that \(f(\E[x]) \leq \E[f(x)]\). Therefore,

\[ L(z) \leq \min_q \sum_{i = 1}^n - \E_{q(z \mid x)} \log p(x_i, z) - \log q(z \mid x_i) \]

docs.title: Density Parameterization
docs.text: Convex optimization via methods like gradient descent are solvers for Machine Learning but density parameterization is a modeler for Machine Learning.

docs.title: Canonical Form
docs.text:
We introduce a base measure \(h(x)\). Then, we introduce a sufficient statistic \(T(x)\) which is used in conjunction with the partition function to express the density. The following form is called the canonical form of an exponential family.

Definition 2.1.1: Exponential Family

\[ p(x) = h(x) \exp(\eta^T T(x) - A(\eta)) \]

Here \(\eta\) parameterizes the distribution, \(T(x)\) is the sufficient statistic, and \(h(x)\) is the base measure.

Definition 2.1.2: Log Partition

\(A(\eta)\) is the log partition function defined as:

\[ A(\eta) = \log \int \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx \]

Then,

\[ \int p(x) dx = \int h(x) \exp(\eta^T T(x)) \cdot \exp(- A(\eta)) dx \]

\(\exp(\eta^T T(x))\) and \(\exp(-A(\eta))\) cancel out so the integrand becomes \(h(x)\) and the density integrates to \(1\).

Since,

\[ \int p(x) dx = 1 = \left [ \int h(x) \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx \right ] \exp(A (\eta)) \]

Then,

\[ \int h(x) \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx = \exp(A(\eta)) \]

docs.title: Conditional Distribution Modeling
docs.text:
We now give some examples of distributions. We model the conditional Gaussian for regression:

\[ y \mid x, \omega \sim \mathcal{N}(\omega^T x, \sigma^2) \]

Then,

\[ P(y \mid x, \omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma}} \exp \left ( - \frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} (y - \omega^T x)^2 \right ) \]

Then, maximizing the log-likelihood becomes:

\[ \text{MLE} = \min_{\omega} \sum_{i = 1}^n ||y_i - \omega^T x_i||^2 \]

We can also model classification using a Bernoulli distribution:

\[ y \mid x, \omega \sim \text{ Bernoulli}(p) \] \[ p = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\omega^T x)} \]

Then,

\[ P(y \mid p) = p^y (1 - p)^{1 - y} \]

docs.title: Members of Exponential Family
docs.text:
We now show that the Bernoulli distribution is in the exponential family.

\[ p(x) = \pi^x (1 - \pi)^{1 - x}, / \pi \in \{0, 1\} \]

Then,

\[ p(x) = \exp(x \log \pi + (1 - x) \log (1 - \pi)) \] \[ p(x) = \exp \left ( x \log \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} + \log (1 - \pi) \right ) \]

Here, \(T(x) = x, \eta = \log(\pi / (1 - \pi)), h(x) = 1\).

Now, the Gaussian.

\[ p(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp( - \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}) \] \[ p(x) = \exp \log \left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp( - \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}) \right ) \] \[ p(x) = \exp \left ( - \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2} - \log \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} \right ) \] \[ p(x) = \exp \left ( - \frac{x^2 - 2 x \mu + \mu^2}{2 \sigma^2} - \log \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} \right ) \]

Here, \(h(x) = 1, T(x) = [x^2, x], \eta = [- \frac{1}{2 \sigma^2}, \frac{\mu^2}{\sigma^2}]\). Then,

\[ A(\eta) = -\frac{\mu^2}{2 \sigma^2} - \log \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} \]

docs.title: Log Partitions, MLE
docs.text:
The log partition function \(A(\eta)\) has important properties. Let's first take its derivative:

\[ \frac{dA(\eta)}{d\eta} = \frac{d}{d\eta} \log \int \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx \]

Let's assume that differentiating through the integral is allowed (dominated convergence theorem). Then,

\[ \frac{dA(\eta)}{d\eta} = \frac{\int \frac{d}{d\eta} \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx}{\int \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx} \] \[ = \frac{\int T(x) \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx}{\exp(A(\eta))} \] \[ = \int T(x) \frac{\exp(\eta^T T(x))}{\int \exp(\eta^T T(x)) dx} \] \[ = \E_{\eta}[T(x)] = \int p_{\eta}(x) T(x) dx \]

where

\[ p_{\eta}(x) = \exp(\eta^T T(x) - A(\eta)) \]

Taking the second derivative provides:

\[ \frac{d^2A(\eta)}{d\eta_a d\eta_b} = \int \frac{d}{d\eta_b} p_{\eta}(x) T_a(x) dx \]

Then,

\[ \frac{d}{d \eta_b} p_{\eta}(x) = p_{\eta}(x) (T_b(x) - \E_{\eta}[T_b(x)]) \] \[ \frac{d^2A(\eta)}{d\eta_a d\eta_n} = \int T_a(x) p_{\eta}(x) (T_b(x) - \E_{\eta}[T_b(x)]) dx \] \[ = \int p_{\eta}(x) T_b(x) T_a(x) - p_{\eta}(x) T_a(x) \E_{\eta}[T_b(x)] \] \[ = \E_{\eta}[T_a(x) T_b(x)] - \E_{\eta}[T_a(x)] \E_{\eta}[T_b(x)] \] \[ = \text{Cov}(T_a(x), T_b(x)) \]

Thus, we can infer two important properties.

First, since the 2nd-order derivatives form a covariance matrix, the Hessian of the log-partition function is PSD (the second-order condition for convexity). Therefore,the log-partition function is convex w.r.t. the natural parameter \(\eta\).

\[ A(t \eta_1 + (1 - t)\eta_2) \leq t A(\eta_1) + (1 - t) A(\eta_2) \]

Second, the \(k\)'th order derivative of the log partition function is the \(k\)'th cumulant of the partition function.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text: We review sampling very briefly.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Consider the supervised learning setting. Bayes rule states that:

\[ p(\theta \mid D) = \frac{p(D \mid \theta) p(\theta)}{p(D)} \]

where \(\theta\) is our parameter set and \(D\) is a dataset. \(p(\theta)\) is a prior over \(\theta\), \(p(D)\) is the marginal likelihood / partition function, \(p(D \mid \theta)\) is the likelihood and \(p(\theta \mid D)\) is the posterior distribution.

Assuming i.i.d.'ness of the dataset \(D\), the likelihood is:

\[ p(D) = \prod_{i = 1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) \]

Then,

\[ p(D) = \int_{\theta} p(D, \theta) d\theta = \int \prod_{i = 1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) p(\theta) d\theta \]

The posterior probability for \(\theta\) is:

\[ p(\theta \mid \{x_i, y_i\}_{i = 1}^n) = \frac{\prod_{i = 1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta)}{\int \prod_{i = 1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta) p(\theta) d\theta} \]

Given some \(x_{\text{test}}\), we can derive the posterior predictive distribution as:

\[ p(y_{\text{test}} \mid x_{\text{test}}, D) = \int_{\Theta} p(y_{\text{test}}, \theta \mid x_{\text{test}}, D) d\theta \] \[ = \int_{\Theta} p(y_{\text{test}} \mid \theta, x_{\text{test}}, D) p(\theta \mid x_{\text{test}}, D) d\theta \] \[ = \int_{\Theta} p(y_{\text{test}} \mid \theta, x_{\text{test}}) p(\theta \mid D) d\theta \]

This integral is very hard to compute since for modern models, we have billions or even trillions of parameters. Thus, we need to find some way to sample \(\theta \mid D\) to compute an estimate of the expected posterior prediction.

docs.title: Monte Carlo
docs.text:
We want to estimate \(\E_p[f(x)] = \int f(x) p(x) dx\).

Definition 3.2.1: Monte Carlo Approximation

Sample points \(x_i \sim p(x)\) such that \(\sum_{i = 1}^n f(x_i) \approx \E_p[f(x)]\).

Important: Properties

The Monte Carlo estimator has good properties. Specifically, it is

  1. Unbiased

    \[ \E[\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i = 1}^k f(x_i)] = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i = 1}^k \E[f(x_i)] = \E_p[f(x)] \]

    All that we require for unbiasedness is identically distributed \(x\)'s, i.e. each \(x_i \sim p(x)\).

  2. Adheres to LLN

    \[ \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i = 1}^k f(x_i) =^{\text{a.s.}} \E_p[f(x)] \]

    This requires almost sure convergence.

  3. Variance tends to \(0\)

    \[ \text{Var}[\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i = 1}^k f(x_i)] = \frac{1}{k^2} \sum_{i = 1}^K \text{Var}(f(x_i)) = \frac{1}{k} \text{Var}(f(x)) \]

    This requires that the \(x\)'s are identically and independently distributed.

docs.title: Basic Sampling
docs.text: I have learned about sampling techniques in a previous machine learning course so I have copied-and-pasted my notes here.

docs.title: Inverse Probability Transform
docs.text:
If we know the inverse CDF of some distribution, then we can sample randomly from that distribution by using transformed samples from a uniform distribution.

If we think of the CDF of a Gaussian distribution, most of the probability density is concentrated around the mean. So the CDF will "jump" near the mean, going from a low value to a high value. Say we we sample uniformly from \([0, 1]\) on the y-axis and walk rightwards until we hit the CDF curve, and then go straight down. We're most likely to hit the CDF curve along the mostly vertical span which, on the \(x\)-axis, constitutes sample points near the mean.

This is nice but requires knowing \(F^{-1}\) of the distribution we wish to sample from which is burdensome.

docs.title: Rejection Sampling
docs.text:
Rejection sampling is essentially sampling from some easy-to-sample-from proposal distribution \(q(x)\) which "covers" our target distribution \(\tilde{p}(x)\). Specifically, we want \(\tilde{p}(x) \leq k q(x)\) for all \(x\).

  • Sample \(x_0 \sim k q(x)\).
  • Sample \(y_0 \sim \text{Uniform}[0, kq(x_0)]\).
  • Accept \(x_0\) if \(y_0 \leq \tilde{p}(x_0)\)

Basically, we know and can sample from \(k q(x)\). By only sampling from the subset of \(k q(x)\) corresponding to \(\tilde{p}(x)\) in proportion to the height of \(\tilde{p}(x)\), we can drawn samples proportionally to \(p(x)\).

Rejection Sampling is a exact-sampling procedure which means the samples it draws exactly follow the target probability distribution.

Naturally, the proposal distribution must be chosen well and the constant \(k\) must be chosen well. However, this method suffers from the curse of dimensionality in that the reject rate increases with the dimension. The accept rate can be computed as the fraction of the area occupied by \(\tilde{p}(x)\) divided by the total are from which we are sampling. So we have

\[ p(\text{Accept}) = \frac{\int \tilde{p}(x) \ dx}{\int k q(x) \ dx} = \frac{\int \tilde{p}(x)}{k} \]

Now assume that \(\tilde{p}(x)\) is normalized and that both distributions are multi-variate Gaussians, i.e. \(q(x) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_q^{\frac{d}{2}} I ), p(x) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_p^{\frac{d}{2}} I)\) and \(\sigma_q^{\frac{d}{2}} \geq \sigma_p^{\frac{d}{2}}\). Then, we have:

\[ p(\text{Accept}) = \frac{\int p(x)}{\int q(x)} = \frac{(2 \pi \sigma_p^2)^d}{(2 \pi \sigma_q^2)^d} = \frac{\sigma_p^{2d}}{\sigma_q^{2d}} \implies k = \left ( \frac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} \right )^D \]

As \(D\) increases to many dimensions (i.e. if we want to sample from the posterior distribution of some neural network), the probability of acceptance decreases very quickly.

docs.title: Importance Sampling
docs.text:
One could view rejection sampling as wasteful given that it discards many samples. Importance sampling gives us a very flexible method for dealing with this problem by essentially assigning weights to samples.

We can write:

\[ \begin{align} \int f(x) p(x) \ dx &= \int f(x) \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} q(x) \ dx \\ &\approx \frac{1}{J} \sum_{j = 1}^J \frac{p(x^{(j)})}{q^{(j)}} f(x^{(j)}) \\ E_p[f(x)] &\approx E_q[f(x) w(x)], w(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \end{align} \]

Basically, the weights are related to how far the sample's probability density is from the boundary between \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\).

It is not necessary that \(q(x)\) be bigger than \(p(x)\) for all \(x\).

The weakness of this method is that the proposal distribution must be chosen extremely carefully.

docs.title: Ancestral Sampling
docs.text:
Ancestral Sampling is essentially sampling from a Bayes net. We have some joint distribution which we specify a partial ordering on.

\[ p(a, b, c, d) = p(a) p(b) p(c \mid a, b) p(d \mid c) \]

The algorithm is extremely simple:

  • Sample from the marginal distributions.
  • Conditioned on the nodes parent, sample from the nodes

This eventually gives us a sample from the joint distribution.

docs.title: EBM
docs.text:
The following is taken from How to Train Your Energy-Based Models by Song & Kingma1.

Probabilistic models require a tractable likelihood. This allows for straightfoward comparison between models and optimization via MLE. Even if the likelihood isn't completely tractable, we can often optimize a variational lower-bound on the likelihood.

Models with tractable likelihoods are constrained in that they are defined as a sampling procedure. Auto-regressive models factorize the joint distribution as a product of conditional distributions. Flow-based models model the data distribution as a sequence of invertible transformations from some base distribution.

Energy-based models only specify the unnormalized negative log-probability called the energy function. The energy function need not integrate to \(1\) and can be parameterized with any non-linear regression function. While they are more flexible, absent an exact likelihood / sampling procedure, training is difficult.

This paper presents three methods for training EBMs - MCMC sampling, Score Matching, and Noise Contrastive Estimation.

Definition 1.1: Energy Based Models

EBMs specify a energy function \(E_{\theta}(x)\). The probability density of some sample \(x\) is given by:

\[ p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{\exp(-E_{\theta}(x))}{Z_{\theta}} \] \[ Z_{\theta} = \int \exp(- E_{\theta}(x)) dx \]

The partition function is constant w.r.t. \(x\) but is a function of \(\theta\).

docs.title: EBM Motivation
docs.text:
We take a brief detour for motivation and show we can derive EBMs from the principle of maximum entropy. Consider the following variational problem over the space of distributions \(\Delta\).

\[ \max_{P \in \Delta} H(P) = \int P(x) \log \frac{1}{P(x)} dx, \ \E_{P(x)}[f(x)] = \mu \]

where \(f\) is some vector of statistics. Why maximum entropy? Suppose you know some data statistics (mean, variance). The maximum entropy principle states to pick the distribution with the highest entropy while still matching those statistics - any lower-entropy distribution is making assumptions about where the distribution is concentrated without evidence.

We can solve MaxEnt via calculus of variations, associating with the functional:

\[ \mathcal{L}(P, \alpha, \eta) = \int P(x) \log \frac{1}{P(x)} dx - \alpha \left( \int P(x) dx - 1 \right) - \left ( \eta^T \E_{P(x)}[f(x)] - \mu \right ) \]

with Lagrange multipliers \(\alpha, \eta\). The entropy attains its maximum when:

\[ \frac{\delta \mathcal{L}}{\delta P} P = \log P(x) + 1 - \alpha - eta^T f(x) = 0 \]

Solving for \(P(x)\), we get:

\[ \log P(x) = \eta^T f(x) + \alpha - 1 \implies P(x) \propto \exp(\eta^T f(x)) \]

To show this is a maximum, you can take the second variation. This is the form of the exponential family and why EBMs take a similar form.

EBMs have advantages. They can be easily combined:

\[ P_1(x) \propto \exp(f_{\theta_1}(x)), P_2(x) \propto \exp(f_{\theta_2}(x)) \]

Then, \(P(x) \propto P_1(x) P_2(x) \propto \exp(f_{\theta_1}(x) + f_{\theta_2}(x))\).

It is also easy to analyze relationships between different coordinates. Suppose \(x, y\) represent different data types. Then, \(P(x, y) \propto \exp(\psi(y)^T \varphi(y))\).

However, they have several disadvantages. They're hard to sample from (MCMC), hard to evaluate (due to intractability of \(Z_{\theta}\)) and hard to learn due to \(Z_{\theta}\).

docs.title: Training - MCMC
docs.text:
We return to the paper and present how train your EBM. Specifically, we can do maximum likelihood training with MCMC sampling, Score Matching, and Noise Contrastive Estimation. We begin with MCMC.

MLE proceeds like \(\E_{x \sim p_{ ext{data}}(x)[ \log p_{ heta}(x)]}\). Maximizing likelihood is equivalent to minimizing KL-divergence between \(p_{ ext{data}}(x)\) and \(p_{ heta}(x)\):

\[ - \E_{x \sim p_{ ext{data}}(x)}[ \log p_{ heta}(x)] = D_{ ext{KL}}(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x)) - \E_{x \sim p_{ ext{data}}(x)}[\log p_{ ext{data}}(x)] \]

The last term is constant w.r.t. \( heta\) so optimizing likelihood is minimizing the KL-divergence between the model's distribution and the data distribution.

EBMs cannot compute likelihoods since they don't have access to \(Z_{ heta}\). However, with MCMC procedures, they can estimate the gradient of the log-likelihood and perform gradient ascent to do likelihood maximization. Intuitively, we want the network to assign low-energy to observed samples and high-energy everywhere else.

In particular,

\[ abla_{ heta} \log p_{ heta}(x) = abla_{ heta} (- E_{ heta}(x) - \log Z_{ heta}) \] \[ = - abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x) - \E_{x \sim p_{ heta}(x)}[- abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x)] \]

The first term on the RHS is \(- abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}[x_{ ext{data}}]\) in other words, seeking to decrease energy at the real data.

The second term is \( abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}[x_{ ext{model}}]\), seeking to increase energy for the model samples. Raising energy just for model samples is enough because that's the area the model currently assigns low energy (when it should assign high energy).

Eventually, once the model samples are similar to the real data, the two gradients cancel out.

The first term can be evaluated via auto-differentiation. Recall that for an exponential family, \( rac{d A(\eta)}{d \eta} = \E_{\eta}[T(x)]\). In this case, the integrand is \(\exp(\eta^T T(x))\) and its derivative w.r.t. \(\eta\) is \(T(x) \exp(\dots)\). In EBMs, the integrand is \(\exp(-E_{ heta}(x))\) and the derivative doesn't have a closed form so it's just \(- abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x) \exp(\dots)\). Therefore,

\[ abla_{ heta} \log Z_{ heta} = \E_{x \sim p_{ heta}(x)}[- abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x)] \]

Using MCMC procedures we can sample \( ilde{x} \sim p_{ heta}(x)\). Then, we can compute our estimate of the gradient of the log-partition function as \( abla_{ heta} \log Z_{ heta}(x) \approx - \sum_{i = 1}^k abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}( ilde{x})\) and do gradient ascent.

Important: Maximum Likelihood vs Marginal Likelihood

The term \(Z( heta)\) is the partition function integrating over data points \(x\). Although it is a normalizing constant, it is distinct from the marginal likelihood which integrates over parameters \( heta\).

We naturally have access to the first term using auto-diff. Since the second term is just the gradient of the EBM w.r.t. \( heta\) where \(x\) is sampled from the model's learned distribution of data, as long as we can draw random samples, we can perform gradient ascent on the log-likelihood w.r.t. \( heta\).

Algorithm 1.2.1: MCMC for MLE

We want to optimize

\[ abla_{ heta} \log p_{ heta}(x) = - abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x) + \E_{x \sim p_{ heta}(x)}[ abla_{ heta} E_{ heta}(x)] \]

Start with \( heta_t\).

  1. Draw real data \(x_1, \dots, x_n \sim p_{ ext{data}}(x)\).

  2. Draw \(m\) samples from the model using Langevin MCMC. Specifically, sample noise \( ilde{x}^0\) and repeat:

    \[ ilde{x}^{k + 1} \leftarrow ilde{x}^k - rac{\epsilon^2}{2} abla_x E_{ heta_t}( ilde{x}^k) + \epsilon z, \ z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \]

  3. Compute gradient estimate

    \[ \hat{ abla}_{ heta_t} = - rac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n abla_{ heta_t} E_{ heta_t}(x_i) + rac{1}{m} \sum_{j = 1}^m abla_{ heta_t} E_{ heta_t}( ilde{x}_j) \]

  4. Update

\[ heta_{t + 1} \leftarrow heta_t + \eta \hat{ abla}_{ heta_t} \]

In short, we use real data to compute the gradient of the negative energy (assign lower energy to real samples). We then generate samples from the network (doing gradient descent on the learned energy landscape) to estimate the gradient of the partition function. Then, we can add the two to get a gradient estimate of the log-likelihood.

Note that this is merely for density estimation, i.e. learning \(p(x)\) to get a generative model. For supervised learning, energy takes the input and label and defines \(E_{ heta}(x, y)\). The normalizing constant sums over labels \(y\). In a discrete classification scenario, thisis just a standard classification model. In a continuous or structured \(y\), the normalizing constant becomes intractable again.

docs.title: Score Matching
docs.text:
If two continuously differentiable real-valued functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) have equal first derivatives everywhere, then \(f(x) = g(x) + C\). When \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are log density functions with equal first derivatives, then they have equivalent normalizing constants and \(f(x) = g(x)\). Therefore, one can learn an EBM by matching the first derivative of its log-PDF with the first derivative of the log-PDF of the data distribution. This is called score matching2.

Recall:

\[ abla_x \log p_{ heta}(x) = - abla_x E_{ heta}(x) - abla_{x} \log Z_{ heta} = - abla_x E_{ heta}(x) \]

since the partition function is constant w.r.t \(x\).

Definition 1.3.1: Score Matching (Fisher)

Let \(p_{ ext{data}}\) be the data distribution. The basic Score Matching objective minimizes the Fisher Divergence:

\[ D_F(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x)) = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)} \left [ rac{1}{2} || abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x) - abla_x \log p_{ heta}(x)||^2 ight ] \]

This is impractical since we typically don't have access to \( abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x)\). Under regularity conditions, the Fisher divergence can be re-written using integration by parts:

\[ D_F(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x)) = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)} \left [ rac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^d \left ( rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i} ight )^2 + rac{\partial^2 E_{ heta}(x)}{(\partial x_i)^2} ight ] \] \[ = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)} [ ext{Tr}( abla^2_x E_{ heta}(x)) + rac{1}{2} || abla_x E_{ heta}(x) ||^2] \]

where \(d\) is the dimensionality of \(x\) and \( abla^2_x E_{ heta}(x)\) is the Hessian of the energy w.r.t. \(x\). Naturally, for high-dimensionality, the Hessian is very expensive to compute.

docs.title: Denoising Score Matching
docs.text:
The score matching objective requires regularity conditions for \(\log p_{ ext{data}}(x)\) (continuously differentiable, finite everywhere). However, a distribution of images is discrete and bounded - \(\log p_{ ext{data}}\) is discontinuous and negative infinity outside the range.

Thus, we can add a bit of noise to each data point, \( ilde{x} = x + \epsilon\). As long as \(p(\epsilon)\) is smooth, the noisy data distribution, \(q( ilde{x}) = \int q( ilde{x} \mid x) p_{ ext{data}}(x) dx\) is smooth and the Fisher divergence \(D_F(q( ilde{x}) \mid \mid p_{ heta}( ilde{x}))\) is a proper objective.

Vincent3 showed that:

\[ D_F(q( ilde{x}) \mid \mid p_{ heta}( ilde{x})) = \E_{q( ilde{x})} \left [ rac{1}{2} || abla_x \log q( ilde{x}) - abla_x \log p_{ heta}( ilde{x}) ||_2^2 ight ] \] \[ = \E_{q(x, ilde{x})} \left [ rac{1}{2} || abla_x \log q( ilde{x} \mid x) - abla_x \log p_{ heta}( ilde{x}) ||_2^2 ight ] \]

This completely avoids the unknown term and second-order derivatives. Formulas can be traced back to Tweedie's formula and SURE (Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimation).

When \(p_{ ext{data}}\) is already well-behaved and satisfies the regularity conditions given by Score Matching, \(D_F(q( ilde{x}) \mid \mid p_{ heta}( ilde{x})) eq D_F(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x))\). The optimal EBM matches the noisy distribution and not the data distribution.

docs.title: NCSN
docs.text:
The following is taken from "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution" by Song & Ermon4.

Score-matching is not scalable due to the computation of \( ext{Tr}( abla_x s_{ heta}(x))\). Denoising score-matching cirucmvents the trace computation but the optimal score network only learns the score of the data distribution at very low noise levels. Sliced score-matching is more expensive than regular score-matching.

Generally, score-based generative modeliing faces two major obstacles.

  1. The manifold hypothesis suggests that the data distribution is clustered on a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional ambient space. First, the score is a gradient taken in the ambient space meaning it is undefined when confining \(x\) to the low-dimensional space. Second, the score-matching objective only provides a consistent estimator when the support of the data distribution is the ambient space.

  2. In regions of low data density, score matching is too low sample to estimate the score accurately. This means that Langevin dynamics (which we use to sample from the model, like in the EBM section) may not be able to traverse low-density regions to go from one mode to another.

Noise Conditional Score Networks find that perturbing the data with random Gaussian noise makes the data distribution easier to model. It means the perturbed data distribution isn't confined to the low-dimensional manifold making score-estimation well-defined. Gaussian noise also fills the low-density regions. By using multiple levels of noise, NCSN achieves a sequence of noise-perturbed distributions which converge to the true data distribution.

Definition 1.4.1: Noise Conditional Score Networks

Consider a sequence of noise levels \(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_L\) where \(\sigma_j / \sigma_{j + 1} > 1\). So \(\sigma_1\) corresponds to a high-noise level and \(\sigma_L\) to a low-noise level.

Let \(q_{\sigma}( ilde{x}) = \int p_{ ext{data}}(x) \ \mathcal{N}( ilde{x} \mid x, \sigma^2 I) \ dx\) be the perturbed data distribution. We want to train a conditional score network to jointly estimate the scores of all perturbed data distributions,

\[ s_{ heta}(x, \sigma) \approx abla_x \log q_{\sigma}(x) \]

The noise distribution is \(q_{\sigma}( ilde{x} \mid x) = \mathcal{N}( ilde{x} \mid x, \sigma^2 I)\). Therefore, \( abla_{ ilde{x}} \log q_{\sigma}( ilde{x} \mid x) = - rac{ ilde{x} - x}{\sigma^2}\). For a given \(\sigma\), the objective (taken from DSM) is:

\[ l( heta, \sigma) = rac{1}{2} \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{ ilde{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(x, \sigma^2 I)} \left [ \left | \left | s_{ heta}( ilde{x}, \sigma) + rac{ ilde{x} - x}{\sigma^2} ight | ight |_2^2 ight ] \]

We combine this for all \(\sigma\) to get:

\[ L( heta, \{\sigma_i\}_{i = 1}^L) = rac{1}{L} \sum_{i = 1}^L \lambda(\sigma_i) l( heta, \sigma_i) \]

where \(\lambda(\sigma_i)\) is a coefficient function dependeing on \(\sigma_i\).

In the loss derived in DSM, the network was trained such that the score of the network matched the score of the single noise-perturbed distribution. Generally, EBMs produce a scalar \(E_{ heta}(x)\) and the score is derived from a backwards pass. NCSNs directly output a \(d\)-dimensional vector and are parameterized to directly predict the score of the noise-perturbed distribution.

The idea of progressively de-noising will be revisited soon. These models are known as diffusion models.

docs.title: AutoEncoder
docs.text:
Reference: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes by Kingma & Welling5.

Definition 2.1.1: Auto-Encoder

An autoencoder is a model that takes some vector \(x\), compresses it into a lower-dimensional vector \(z\) and decompresses \(z\) back to \(x\). Here,

\[ z = h_{\phi}(x), x' = f_{\theta}(z) \]

Here, \(h_{\phi}\) is an encoder and \(f_{\theta}\) is a decoder. Typically, both functions are neural networks.

The parameters \(\{\theta, \phi\}\) are learned jointly, typically via something like MSE:

\[ L_{\text{AE}}(\theta, \phi) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n (x_i - f_{\theta}(h_{\phi}(x_i)))^2 \]

docs.title: Variational Bayes
docs.text:
Variational Auto-Encoders are like probabilistic versions of autoencoders. The following derivation is taken from From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE by Lilian Weng (Lil'Log)6.

A VAE can be viewed as a directed PGM \(z \to x\). Instead of taking some input \(x\) into a fixed vector \(z\), we map it to a posterior distribution \(p_{\theta}(z \mid x)\). This requires a prior \(p(z)\) and a likelihood \(p_{\theta}(x \mid z)\). The likelihood function is a conditional distribution parameterized by \(\theta\) called the decoder.

Suppose we know the real \(\theta^*\) for this distribution. To sample some \(x_i\), we:

  1. Sample \(z_i \sim p(z)\).

  2. Sample \(x_i \sim p_{\theta^*}(x \mid z = z_i)\).

The optimal parameter \(\theta^*\) is the one that maximizes the probability of real data samples:

\[ \theta^* = \argmax_{\theta} \prod_{i = 1}^n p_{\theta}(x_i) \] \[ = \argmax_{\theta} \sum_{i = 1}^n \log p_{\theta}(x_i) \] \[ = \argmax_{\theta} \sum_{i = 1}^n \log \int p_{\theta}(x_i \mid z) p(z) dz \]

This integral is analytically intractable but crucially, hard to estimate. We want to estimate \(\int p_{\theta}(x_i \mid z) p(z) dz\). Ideally, we could just sample \(z \sim p(z)\) and then compute the density \(p(x_i \mid z = z)\) and multiply the densities together. Then, we should just average those to estimate \(p_{\theta}(x_i)\).

The problem is that \(p_{\theta}(x_i \mid z = z), z \sim p(z)\) is nearly always \(0\). Randomly sampled latents from the prior basically have zero chance of producing the observed data. Generally, the \(z\)'s that are likely to produce the observed \(x\) occupy a tiny fraction of the prior's probability so the estimate has very high variance. As a consequence, rejection-sampling also won't work since our rejection rate will be too high.

We need to do importance sampling. Ideally, we want some tractable proposal distribution \(q(z)\) which puts a lot of probability on the \(z\)'s that could generate \(x_i\)'s.

\[ p_{\theta}(x_i) = \E_{z \sim q(z)} \left [ p_{\theta}(x_i \mid z) \cdot \frac{p(z)}{q(z)} \right ] \]

The best proposal is the posterior \(p_{\theta}(z \mid x_i)\) as it ensures that the weights are just the likelihoods themselves \(p_{\theta}(x_i)\). However,

\[ p_{\theta}(z \mid x) = \frac{p_{\theta}(x \mid z) p(z)}{p_{\theta}(x)} \]

so this quantity assumes we already have access to the likelihood \(p_{\theta}(x)\). Instead, we can train an encoder network \(q_{\phi}(z \mid x)\) meant to approximate the posterior distribution. This can stabilize our likelihood estimate.

We can use KL-Divergence to do this (specifically, the reverse KL):

\[ \min_{\phi} D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p_{\theta}(z \mid x)) \]

We need to use the reverse KL as we do not have the ability to sample from \(p_{\theta}(z \mid x)\) and the forward KL is an expectation over the true posterior. The goal here is to isolate all of the terms we cannot compute on one side. This involves \(p_{\theta}(x)\) and \(p_{\theta}(z \mid x)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} &= \int q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}{p_{\theta}(z \mid x)} dz \\ &= \int q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x) p_{\theta}(x)}{p_{\theta}(z, x)} dz \\ &= \int q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \left (\log p_{\theta}(x) + \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}{p_{\theta}(z, x)} \right ) dz \\ &= \log p_{\theta}(x) + \int q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}{p_{\theta}(z, x)} dz \\ &= \log p_{\theta}(x) + \int q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}{p_{\theta}(x \mid z) p(z)} \\ &= \log p_{\theta}(x) + \E_{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)} \left [ \log \frac{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}{p(z)} - \log p_{\theta}(x \mid z) \right ] \\ &= \log p_{\theta}(x) + D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p(z)) - \E_{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}[\log p_{\theta}(x \mid z)] \end{aligned} \]

Rearranging, we have:

\[ \log p_{\theta}(x) - D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p_{\theta}(z \mid x)) = \E_{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}[\log p_{\theta}(x \mid z)] - D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p(z)) \]

When learning the true distribution, we want to maximize the log-likelihood while minimizing the difference between the approximated and true posterior. Thus, our loss is:

\[ \begin{aligned} L_{\text{VAE}}(\theta, \phi) &= - \log p_{\theta}(x) + D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p_{\theta}(z \mid x)) \\ &= - \E_{q_{\phi}(z \mid x)}[\log p_{\theta}(x \mid z)] + D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p(z)) \end{aligned} \]

This loss function is known as the ELBO or the evidence lower bound. It's a lower-bound - since KL-Divergence is always non-negative:

\[ - L_{\text{VAE}}(\theta, \phi) = \log p_{\theta}(x) - D_{\text{KL}}(q_{\phi}(z \mid x) \mid \mid p_{\theta}(z \mid x)) \leq \log p_{\theta}(x) \]

By minimizing the loss, we are maximizing a lower bound on the log-likelihood.

docs.title: Reparameterization
docs.text:
The ELBO involves expectations which involve sampling \(z \sim q_{\phi}(z \mid x)\). In this form, we cannot backpropagate to compute gradients. We use the reparameterization trick. Suppose \(z \sim q_{\phi}(z \mid x_i) = \mathcal{N}(z; \mu_i, \sigma^2_i I)\). We can set \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \mathcal{N}(0, I)\).

We directly set the encoder to output two \(d\)-dimensional vectors, corresponding to the mean \(\mu_{\phi}\) and the diagonal covariance \(\log \sigma_{\phi}\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In short, in order to do MLE, we needed to estimate the likelihood \(p_{\theta}(x)\) which would've required marginalizing over all latents \(z\). This integral is analytically intractable and hard to estimate via sampling - \(z\)'s sampled from the prior are very unlikely to produce the observed \(x\) so our likelihood estimate of \(p_{\theta}(x)\) is very high variance. We need to do importance sampling and choose an appropriate proposal distribution. Ideally, we would like to sample from the posterior but that requires knowing the likelihood \(p_{\theta}(x)\) in the first place.

Instead, we can optimize the reverse KL-divergence between a learned posterior and the actual posterior. After isolating inaccessible terms, we end up with a regularized reconstruction objective which jointly trains both the encoder and decoder at the same time (minimizing an upper bound (NELBO) on the NLL). The result is a generative model which is able to produce realistic samples starting with latents sampled from the prior.

docs.title: Sliced Score Matching
docs.text:
Instead of minimizing Fisher divergence, Sliced Score Matching minimizes the sliced Fisher divergence.

Definition 5.1.1: Sliced Score Matching

Randomly sample a projection \(v\). Take the inner-product between \(v\) and the two scores and compare the scalars. This forms an objective called Sliced Fisher Divergence:

\[ D_{SF}(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x)) = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{p(v)} \left [ rac{1}{2} v^T( abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x) - abla_x \log p_{ heta}(x)) ight ] \] \[ = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{p(v)} \left [ rac{1}{2} \left (v^T abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x) - v^T abla_x \log p_{ heta}(x) ight ) ight ] \]

Again, we don't have access to the gradients of the data distribution. So the implicit form is:

\[ = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{p(v)} \left [ rac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^d \left ( rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i} v_i ight )^2 + \sum_{i = 1}^d \sum_{j = 1}^d rac{\partial^2 E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} v_i v_j ight ] + C \]

The second term involves second-derivatives of the \(E_{ heta}(x)\) but that can be computed efficiently in \(O(d)\). This is because:

\[ \sum_{i = 1}^d \sum_{j = 1}^d rac{\partial^2 E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} v_i v_j = \sum_{i = 1}^d rac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \left ( \sum_{j = 1}^d rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_j} v_j ight) v_i \]

The term in the parantheses does not depend on \(i\) so we only need to compute it once with a \(O(d)\) computation and another \(O(d)\) computation for the outer sum. For many \(p(v)\), the SSM objective can be evaluated in closed form. When \(p(v) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), we have:

\[ \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{p(v)} \left [ rac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^d \left ( rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i} v_i ight )^2 = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \left [ rac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^d \left ( rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i} ight )^2 ight ] ight ] \]

Therefore,

\[ D_{SF}(p_{ ext{data}}(x) \mid \mid p_{ heta}(x)) = \E_{p_{ ext{data}}} \E_{v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left [ rac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^d \left ( rac{\partial E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i} ight )^2 + \sum_{i = 1}^d \sum_{j = 1}^d rac{\partial^2 E_{ heta}(x)}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} v_i v_j ight ] \]

with a constant \(C\) omitted. The left-term is the squared norm of the gradient of the energy w.r.t. \(x\).

docs.title: Setting
docs.text:
LLMs model joint distribution over sequences of tokens auto-regressively using the chain law of probability.

\[ p_{\theta}(x_{2:T} \mid x_1) = \prod_{t = 1}^{T - 1} p_{\theta}(x_{t + 1} \mid x_{\leq t}) \] \[ = p_{\theta}(x_2 \mid x_1) p_{\theta}(x_3 \mid x_2, x_1) \dots p_{\theta}(x_{T} \mid x_1 \dots x_{T - 1}) \]

Note that during training, transformers recieve the true prefix - this is called teacher forcing. Like many other ML settings, we train using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) done by minimizing negative log-likelihood of cross-entropy. We also normalize per sequence length.

\[ L(\theta) = - \frac{1}{T - 1} \E_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}} \left [ \log p_{\theta}(x) \right ] = - \frac{1}{T - 1} \E_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}} \left [ \sum_{i = 1}^{T - 1} \log p_{\theta}(x_{t + 1} \mid x_{\leq t}) \right ] \]

In other words, the model \(\theta\) is punished for assigning low probabilities to observed tokens.

Naturally, this expectation is intractable so we need to average over available examples. A more intuitive measure of this negative likelihood is called perplexity.

Important: Perplexity

Perplexity is defined as \(\exp(L)\) and is equivalent to the uncertainty you'd experience when rolling a die. A perplexity of \(20\) means you're choosing a token from a uniform distribution over \(20\) choices (rolling a \(20\) sided die). See this blog post for more.

Evaluating LLMs is tricky. There have been times where the sample qualities achieve lower perplexity (as evaluated by a larger model which we take to provide the ground-truth) but also lower sample diversity. For example, a model which simply repeats many common tokens (BOS, EOS, "the") may achieve good perplexity according to a weak evaluator like GPT2.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
To optimize this loss function with respect to the parameters \(\theta\), we use gradient descent (where the gradient is computed over a batch of sequences). There are many resources about backpropagation available but the idea is to simply use the chain rule from calculus.

An epoch is a single pass over the training dataset. In training my language diffusion models, we used 33 epochs over LM1B, a dataset of about 1 billion tokens.

A crucial hyperparameter in the optimizer is the learning rate. Essentially, gradient descent computes:

\[ \theta^{(i + 1)} = \theta_i - \eta \nabla L_{\theta_i} \]

where \(\eta\) is the learning-rate - essentially, how large of a step do we take in the gradient direction. If \(\eta\) is too small, we will never reach a good loss value. If \(\eta\) is too big, we may "overshoot" the minima we're aiming for.

Warmup starts with small updates and increases scale early in training. Decay decreases it later.

More advanced optimization methods (SGD with Momentum, AdamW) seek to stabilize gradient-based training (i.e. keeping running direction from past gradients or normalizing moment-estimates for the gradients).

Weight decay shrinks selected parameters towards \(0\). In AdamW, it is decoupled from gradient's moving averages.

Gradient Clipping tries to avoid taking huge steps even when a single batch can yield huge gradients.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: Gradient norms, parameter / activation magnitudes (RMS). The time when the metric is measured also matters - pre-clipping gradients, post-update parameters, etc.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
QK-normalization applies RMSNorm to each attention head's query / key vector before computing the dot-product.

SwiGLU computes:

\[ \text{SwiGLU}(x) = (Wx+b)*\text{Swish}(Vx+c) \] \[ \text{Swish}(Vx+c) = (Vx + c) \sigma(\beta (Vx + c)) \]

where \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\).

docs.title: Metric Space
docs.text:
Definition 1.1: Metric space

A metric space is a pair \((M, d)\) consisting of a set of points \(M\) and a metric \(d: M \times M \to \R_{\geq 0}\). \(d\) is symmetric, positive-definite, and satisfies the triangle-inequality.

Example 1.1: \(\R^N\)

  1. The real line \(\R\) is a metric space under \(d(x, y) = |x - y|\).

  2. \(\R^2\) is a metric space where \(d((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = \sqrt{(x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2}\).

This metric allows for very natural definitions of convergence and continuity.

Definition 1.2: Convergence

Let \((x_n)_{n \geq 1}\) be a sequence of points in a metric space \((M, d)\). We say that \(x_n\) converges to \(x\) if for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there is an integer \(N_{\epsilon}\) such that for each \(n \geq N_{\epsilon}\),

\[ d(x_n, x) < \epsilon \]

Definition 1.3: Continuity

Let \(M = (M, d_M), N = (N, d_N)\) be metric spaces. A function \(f: M \to N\) is continuous at a point \(p \in M\) if for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[ d_M(x, p) < \epsilon \implies d_N(f(x), f(p)) < \delta \]

An equivalent condition is that of sequential continuity. A function \(f: M \to N\) is continuous at \(p \in M\) if and only if the following property holds: if \(x_1, x_2, \dots\) is a sequence in \(M\) converging to \(p\), then the sequence \(f(x_1), f(x_2), \dots\) in \(N\) converges to \(f(p)\).

Definition 1.4: Bounded

A metric space \(M\) is bounded iff for every point \(p \in M\), there is a radius \(R\) such that for all $q \in $M, $d(p, q) \leq $.

Prototypical example: \([0, 1]\) is bounded but \(\R\) is not.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Topological space define notions like continuity, open, and closed without a metric. A metric naturally defines open sets but we can start with the open sets andn forget the metric entirely.

Definition 2.1: Topological space

A topological space is a pair \((X, \mathcal{T})\) where \(X\) is a set of points and \(\mathcal{T}\) is the topology which consists of subsets of \(X\) called the open sets of \(X\). Specifically,

  1. \(\emptyset, X \in \mathcal{T}\).
  2. Finite intersectsions of open sets are in \(\mathcal{T}\).
  3. Arbitrary unions of open sets are in \(\mathcal{T}\).

Definition 2.2: Open Neighborhood

An open neighborhood of a point \(x \in X\) is an open set \(U\) which contains \(x\).

Definition 2.3: Continuity

A function \(f: X \to Y\) of topological spaces is continuous at \(p \in X\) if the pre-image of any open neighborhood of \(f(p)\) contains an open-neighborhood of \(p\).

Example 2.1: Hausdorff space

A topological space \(X\) is Hausdorff if for any two distinct points \(p, q \in X\), there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(p\) and \(V\) of \(q\) which do not intersect.

An intuition behind Hausdorff spaces is that these spaces have resolution - we can always zoom in to "tell points apart". All metric spaces are Hausdorff. Consider two distinct points \(x, y\) where \(d(x, y) = \epsilon, \epsilon > 0\). We can draw \(\epsilon / 4\)-neighborhoods around \(x, y\) which do not intersect. Hence, any metric space is Hausdorff.

Compactness generalizes the idea of being closed and bounded in a topological space.

Definition 2.4: Open Cover

An open cover of a topological space \(X\) is a collection of open sets \(\{U_{\alpha}\}\) which covers it.

\[ X = \bigcup U_{\alpha} \]

A sub-cover is a subset of \(U_{\alpha}\) which still overs \(X\).

Note that equality comes from the "universe" being \(X\).

Definition 2.5: Compact

A topological space \(X\) is quasicompact if every open cover has a finite subcover. It is compact if it is also Hausdorff.

docs.title: Measures
docs.text:
Consider a non-empty set \(\Omega\).

Definition 3.1.1: \(\sigma\)-algebra

A collection \(\mathcal{S}\) of subsets of \(\Omega\) for which:

  1. \(\Omega \in \mathcal{S}\).
  2. \(A \in \mathcal{S} \implies A^C \in \mathcal{S}\).
  3. \(S_1, S_2, \dots \in \mathcal{S} \implies S_1 \cup S_2 \cup \dots \in \mathcal{S}\).

The pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{S})\) is called a measurable space.

Definition 3.1.2: Measure

Let \(S\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\). A map \(\mu: S \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if:

  1. \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\).
  2. \(S_1, S_2, \dots,\) are pairwise-disjoint implies that \(\mu(S_1 \cup S_1 \cup \dots) = \sum_{i} \mu(S_i)\).

The \(\sigma\)-algebra selects which events \(S \subset \Omega\) we can measure. For the trivial \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(\{\emptyset, \Omega\}\), all we know is that \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0, \mu(\Omega) = 1\).

If \(a^{-1}\) exists, it is unique.

Sup. \(a^{-1}a = 1\), \(b^{-1}a = 1\). Then

Inverses multiply in opposite order.

Sup. \(a, b\) invertible. WTS that \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

\[ \begin{aligned} (ab)(ab)^{-1} &= 1 \\ (ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) &= \\ a(bb^{-1})a^{-1} &= \\ aa^{-1} &= 1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad (ab)^{-1} &= b^{-1}a^{-1} \end{aligned} \]
By def'n, an inv. of \(a\) is some elem \(b\) s.t. \(ab = ba = 1\). See 1.3 for example.

Consider \(s(n): \N \to \N\) where \(s(n) = n + 1\). WTS \(s(n)\) has no right inverse but inf. many left inverses.

Let \(f: \N \to \N\) be our candidate inverse. \(s(n)\) has no right inverse. We require that \(s \circ f(n) = n\). But there is no natural number \(f(1)\) such that \(s \circ f(1) = 1\) since \(1\) is the smallest element in \(\N\). Therefore, \(s\) has no right inverse.

However, \(s\) has infinitely many left inverses. We require that \(f \circ s(n) = n\). So \(f(2) = 1, f(3) = 2, \dots\). However, \(f(1)\) is free to vary. Therefore, there are an infinite number of left inverses of \(s\).

Let \(k' = |ba|\). Then, \(k' \leq k\). By symmetry, we can show that \(k \leq k'\) (repeat the above trick in the opposite direction). Therefore, \(k' = k\) and \(|ab| = |ba|\).

Describe all groups \(G\) that contain no proper subgroup.

A proper subgroup is a subgroup which is neither the whole group nor the trivial group (just the identity). This is all cyclic groups which have prime orders.

Clearly, any divisors of \(|G|\) other than \(1\) don't generate \(G\) as they cycle through \(G\) once reaching \(|G|\). But neither does \(x^4\) since the cycle goes \(x^4, x^2, x^6, x^4\). Only elements with exponents which are relatively prime to \(|G|\) generate \(G\). So if \(|G| = 6\), then, \(\{x, x^5\}\). If \(|G| = 5\), then \(\{x, x^2, x^3, x^4\}\) generate \(G\). If \(|G| = 8\), then \(\{x, x^3, x^5, x^7\}\) generate \(G\).

--- Skipping a ---

b) Show that elementary matrices of the first type generate \(\text{SL}_n(\R)\). Do the \(2 \times 2\) case first.

We'll show that you can convert arbitrary elements of \(\text{SL}_n(\R)\) into \(I\) using only left-multiplication by first-type elementary matrices. These matrices correspond to row addition / subtraction which does not affect determinants. Consider the \(2 \times 2\) case first. Then, we have \(x \in \text{SL}_n(\R)\) where:

\[ x = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \]

where \(ad - bc = 1\). Suppose \(c \neq 0\). Then, left-multiply by:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & (1 - a)/c \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b + d(1 - a)/c \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -c & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b + d(1 - a)/c \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b + d(1 - a)/c \\ 0 & d -c(b + d(1 - a)/c) \end{bmatrix} \]

Observe that the bottom-right element reduces to \(ad - bc = 1\). So we have:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & b + d(1 - a)/c \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

We can easily clear the top-right element since elementary matrices of the first type do row substitution. Since we can convert arbitrary \(2 \times 2\) matrices with determinant \(1\) into \(I_2\) with just first-type elementary matrices, we can generate those matrices by inverting the first-type elementary matrices (which themselves are first-type elementary matrices).

Next, we generalize by induction. Suppose it's true for \(n - 1\). We've shown it true for the base case \(n = 2\). Consider \(n \times n\) matrix \(A\).

Since \(\det(A) = 1\), the first column must have some non-zero entry. Suppose there exists some non-zero \(a\) in the first column. Via row-substitution, we can introduce a second element \(ta\) into a different row. Using the same trick as in the \(2 \times 2\) case, we can convert the top-left element of \(A\) and clear out the column. Then, the matrix looks like

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{ junk } \\ 0 & B \end{bmatrix} \]

where \(B\) is the submatrix. Since we've only done row substitutions, we haven't changed the determinant of \(B\). Via cofactor expansion where \(a_{11} = 1\), we know that \(\det(B) = 1\). By the induction assumption, we can reduce \(B\) in the same way. Therefore, \(A\) can be generated by first-type elementary matrices and by induction first-type elementary matrices generate \(\text{SL}_n(\R)\) for all \(n\).
