docs.title: Isometries
docs.text:
The distance between points of \(\R^{n}\) is the length \(u - v\) of the vector \(u - v\).

Definition 6.1.1: Isometry

An isometry of \(\R^{n}\) is a distance-preserving map \(f: \R^n \to \R^{n}\) such that for all \(u, \in \R^n\),

\[ |f(u) - f(v)| = |u - v| \]

An isometry will map a figure to a congruent figure.

Example 6.1.1: Isometries

  • Orthogonal linear operators are isometries. Since \(\varphi\) is linear, it follows that \(\varphi(u) - \varphi(v) = \varphi(u - v)\). Then,

    \[ |\varphi(u - v)| = |u - v| \]

    hence orthogonal operators preserve distances.

  • Translation \(t_a\) be a vector \(a\), \(t_a(x) = x + a\) is an isometry (as the vectors \(a\) cancel out).

  • Composition of isometries is an isometry.

Recall the definition of an orthogonal matrix. \(A\) is an orthogonal matrix provided that \(A^T A = I \iff A^T = A^{-1} \iff Ax \cdot Ay = x \cdot y \iff \det(A) = \pm 1 \iff A\)'s columns form an orthonormal basis of \(R^n\).

Crucially, we will use the property of preserving dot-products, i.e. \(Ax \cdot Ay\).

Theorem 6.1.2: Isometry Conditions

The following conditions on \(\varphi: \R^n \to \R^n\) are equivalent.

  • a. \(\varphi\) is an isometry that fixes the origin \(\varphi(0) = 0\).
  • b. \(\varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(w) = v \cdot w\) for all \(v, w\).
  • c. \(\varphi\) is an orthogonal linear operator.

We know that \(c \implies a\).

Lemma 6.1.3

Let \(x, y \in \R^n\). If \(x \cdot x = x \cdot y = y \cdot y\), then \(x = y\).

Proof

Suppose \(x \cdot x = x \cdot y = y \cdot y\). Then,

\[ (x - y) \cdot (x - y) = x \cdot x + y \cdot y - 2 x \cdot y = 0 \implies x = y \]

Now, we prove that \(b \implies c\).

Proof

Let \(\varphi\) be a map that preserves dot-products. Then, it will be orthogonal provided that it is a linear operator. So we need to show that \(\varphi(cx) = c \varphi(x)\) and \(\varphi(x + y) = \varphi(x) + \varphi(y)\).

Suppose \(w = u + v\). We want to show that \(\varphi(w) = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v)\). To show this, it suffices to show that \(\varphi(w) \cdot \varphi(w) = \varphi(w) \cdot (\varphi(u) + \varphi(v)) = (\varphi(u) + \varphi(v)) \cdot (\varphi(u) + \varphi(v))\).

Then, it suffices to show that:

\[ \varphi(w) \cdot \varphi(w) = \varphi(w) \cdot \varphi(u) + \varphi(w) \cdot \varphi(v) = \varphi(u) \cdot \varphi(u) + \varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(v) + 2 \varphi(u) \cdot \varphi(v) \]

Since \(\varphi\) preserves dot-products, we just need to show that:

\[ w \cdot w = w \cdot u + w \cdot v = u \cdot u + v \cdot v + 2 u \cdot v \]

Since \(w = (u + v)\), we have that \(w \cdot w = w \cdot (u + v) = (u + v) \cdot (u + v)\). Therefore, \(\varphi(w) = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v)\).

The proof for \(\varphi(cv) = c \varphi(v)\) sets \(u = cv\) and shows that \(\varphi(u) = c \varphi(v)\) and is analogous.

Next, we show that \(a \implies b\).

Proof

Let \(\varphi\) be an isometry that fixes the origin. Then,

\[ (\varphi(u) - \varphi(v)) \cdot (\varphi(u) - \varphi(v)) = (u - v) \cdot (u - v) \]

Substitute \(v = 0\). Since \(\varphi(0) = 0\), it follows that \(\varphi(u) \cdot \varphi(u) = u \cdot u\). Similarly, \(\varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(v) = v \cdot v\). Expanding, we get:

\[ \varphi(u) \cdot \varphi(u) + \varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(v) - 2 \varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(u) = u \cdot u + v \cdot v - 2 u \cdot v \]

Canceling, we get:

\[ \varphi(v) \cdot \varphi(u) = u \cdot v \]

Corollary 6.1.4: Isometry Composition

Every isometry \(f\) of \(\R^n\) is the composition of an orthogonal linear operator and a translation. If \(f\) is an isometry and \(f(0) = a\), then \(f = t_a \varphi\) where \(t_a\) is a translation and \(\varphi\) is an orthogonal linear operator. This expression for \(f\) is unique.

Proof

Let \(f\) be an isometry and \(a = f(0)\). Let \(\varphi = t_{- a} f\). Then, \(t_a \varphi = f\). Since \(\varphi\) is the composition of isometries \(t_{- a}\) and \(f\), it's an isometry. \(\varphi\) also fixes the origin, \(\varphi(0) = t_{-a} f(0) = t_{-a} a = 0\). Since \(\varphi\) is an isometry which fixes the origin, it is an orthogonal linear operator. The expression \(f = t_a \varphi\) is unique - since \(\varphi(0) = 0\), we have \(a = f(0) \implies \varphi = t_{- a} f\).

Can we compose isometries together? We know that the composition of orthogonal operators is an orthogonal operator.

Clearly, \(t_a t_b = t_{a + b}\). We also have that \(\varphi t_a = t_{\varphi(a)} \varphi\).

\[ \varphi t_a(x) = \varphi(a + x) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(x) = t_{\varphi(a)} \varphi(x) \]

Corollary 6.1.5: Isometry Group

The set of all isometries of \(\R^n\) forms a group \(M_n\) with composition of functions as its law of composition.

Proof

The composition of isometries is an isometry. The inverse of an isometry is an isometry too since orthogonal operators and translations are invertible so if \(f = t_a \varphi\), then

\[ f^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} t_a^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} t_{- a} \]

This is a composition of isometries so \(f^{-1}\) is an isometry.

The composition of isometries:

\[ t_a \varphi t_b \phi (x) = t_a \varphi(b + \phi(x)) = a + \varphi(b) + \varphi \phi(x) = t_{a + \varphi(b)} \varphi \phi(x) \]

\(O_n\) is the group of \(n \times n\) orthogonal matrices (product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal and the transpose (inverse) is orthogonal). \(O_n\) is a subgroup of \(\text{GL}_n\).

Proposition 6.1.6: Homomorphism

There is a map \(\pi: M_n \to O_n\) defined by dropping the translation part of an isometry. Specifically, if \(f = t_a \varphi\), then \(\pi(f) = \varphi\). This map \(\pi\) is a surjective homomorphism where \(\text{Ker}(\pi) = T = \{t_v\}\), the set of translations which is a normal subgroup of \(M_n\).

Proof

It's clear that \(\pi\) is surjective. We need to show that \(\pi(fg) = \pi(f) \pi(g)\). Suppose \(f = t_a \varphi, g = t_b \phi\). Then,

\[ \pi(f) \pi(g) = \varphi \phi \] \[ \pi(fg) = \pi(t_a \varphi t_b \phi) = \pi(t_{a + \varphi(b)} \varphi \phi) = \varphi \phi \]

Therefore, \(\pi(fg) = \pi(f) \pi(g)\) so \(\pi\) is a homomorphism.

Let \(P\) be an \(n\)-dimensional space. The formula \(t_a \varphi\) depends on the choice of coordinates. How does the formula change when coordinates are changed? We allow changes of coordinates via isometry.

Consider isometry \(f, p \in P\) and \(q = f(p)\). When we introduce coordinates \(P\) is identified with \(\R^n\) and \(p, q\) have coordinates as \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n), y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)\). Then, \(q = f(p)\) translates to \(y = m(x) = t_a \varphi(x)\).

Let \(\eta\) be the isometry performing a change of coordinates. Specifically, \(\eta\) maps new coordinates back to the old coordinates. Then, the new coordinate vectors for \(p, q\) are \(x', y'\). Then, \(m'\) for \(f\) is \(m'(x') = y'\). Substitute \(\eta(x') = x, \eta(y') = y\) into the equation \(m(x) = y\) obtaining \(m \eta(x') = \eta(y') \implies \eta^{-1} m \eta(x') = y'\). So the new formula is the conjugate:

\[ m' = \eta^{-1} m \eta \]

Corollary 6.1.7

The homomorphism \(\pi: M_n \to O_n\) doesn't change when the origin is shifted by translation.

If \(\eta = t_v\), then \(m' = t_{- v} m t_v\). Since the translations are in the kernel of \(\pi\) and since \(\pi\) is a homomorphism, \(\pi(m') = \pi(m)\).

Finally, we consider orientation. The determinant of orthogonal operator \(\varphi\) on \(\R^n\) is \(\pm 1\). The operator is orientation-preserving if \(\det(\varphi) = 1\) and orientation-reversing if \(\det(\varphi) = -1\). Similarly, an isometry \(f = t_a \varphi\) is called orientation-preserving or reverseing if \(\varphi\) is orientation preserving or reversing.

The map \(\sigma: M_n \to \{\pm 1\}\) that sends orientation-preserving isometries to \(1\) and orientation-reserving isometries to \(-1\) is a group homomorphism.

docs.title: Plane Isometries
docs.text:
We consider isometries of the plane. Let \(M\) be the group of isometries of the plane. To compute in this group, we'll choose some special isometries as generators and obtain relations among them.

Recall - we say that a set \(U\) generates a group \(G\) provided that every element \(g \in G\) can be expressed as a product of some string of elements in \(U\).

Pick a coordinate system and identify the plane \(P\) with \(\R^2\). We choose as generators the translations, rotations around the origin and reflection across the \(e_1\) axis. Let the rotation angle \( heta\) be written as \( ho_{ heta}\) and the reflection angle about the \(e_1\) axis be \(r\). These are linear operators.

  1. Translation \(t_a\) by a vector \(t_a(x) = x + a\).

  2. Rotation \( ho_{ heta}\) by \( heta\) about the origin is:

\[ ho_{ heta} = egin{bmatrix} \cos heta & - \sin heta \ \sin heta & \cos heta \end{bmatrix} \]
  1. Reflection about the \(e_1\)-axis:
\[ r = egin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]

These three elements \((t_a, ho_{ heta}, r)\) can generate all other isometries (rotation about a point other than the origin, reflection about other lines, etc).

Theorem 6.2.1: Uniqueness

Let \(m\) be an isometry of the plane. Then, \(m = t_v ho_{ heta}\) or \(m = t_v ho_{ heta} r\) for a uniquely determined vector \(v\) and angle \( heta\).

Proof

Any isometry \(m\) can be written uniquely as \(m = t_v \varphi\) where \(\varphi\) is an orthogonal operator. The orthogonal linear operators on \(\R^2\) are the rotations \( ho_{ heta}\) and the reflections about lines through the origins, of the form \( ho_{ heta} r\).

An isometry of the form \(t_v ho_{ heta}\) preserves orientation while \(t_v ho_{ heta} r\) reverses orientation.

Computation can be done as follows:

  • \( ho_{ heta} t_v = t_{ ho_{ heta}(v)} ho_{ heta}\).
  • \(r t_v = t_{r(v)} r\)
  • \(r ho_{ heta} = ho_{- heta} r\)
  • \(t_v t_w = t_{v + w}\). \( ho_{ heta} ho_{\eta} = ho_{ heta + \eta}\). \(rr = 1\).

We now describe the plane isometries geometrically.

Theorem 6.2.2: Isometry Forms

Every isometry of the plane has one of the following forms.

  • Orientation-preserving: Translation, rotation.

  • Orientation-reversing: Reflection, glides (reflect along some line, then translate).

Glide Symmetry.

This theorem has interesting consequences - composing rotations about two different points is just a single rotation about a third point.

The composition of reflections about nonparallel lines \(\ell_1, \ell_2\) is a rotation about the intersection point \(p = \ell_1 \cap \ell_2\). This follows from the theorem since the composition is orientation-preserving and it fixes \(p\). Composition of reflections about parallel lines is translation by a vector orthogonal to the lines.

Proof

Let \(f\) be an isometry that preserves orientation but isn't a translation. Then, \(f\) is a rotation about some point. We choose coordinates to write the formula for \(f\) as \(m = t_a ho_{ heta}\). Since \(m\) isn't a translation, \( heta eq 0\).

Lemma 6.2.3

An isometry \(f\) with the form \(m = t_a ho_{ heta}\) where \( heta eq 0\) is a rotation through \( heta\) about a point in the plane.

Proof

Let \( ho = ho_{ heta}\). We change coordinates by a translation \(t_p\). We wish to choose \(p\) so that the new formula for \(f\) becomes \(m' = ho\). Then, \(f\) will be a rotation with \( heta\) about \(p\).

The rule is that \(t_p(x') = x\) so \(m' = t_{-p} m t_p = t_{-p} t_a ho t_p = t_{a - p} ho t_p\). Let \(b = a - p + ho(p)\) so \(m' = t_b ho\). We want to choose \(p\) such that \(b = 0\). We simply need to solve \(p - ho(p) = a\) or \((I - ho) p = a\).

Let \(I\) be the identity, \(c = \cos heta\) and \(s = \sin heta\). Then,

\[ I - ho = egin{bmatrix} 1 - c & s \ -s & 1 - c \end{bmatrix} \]

with determinant \((1-c)^2 + s^2 = 1 - 2c + c^2 + s^2 = 2 - 2c\). This determinant is \(0\) when \(2 - 2 \cos heta = 0\) or when \( heta = 0\). Since \( heta eq 0\) (by assumption), the equation \((I - ho)p = a\) has a unique solution for \(p\).

The point \(P\) is the fixed point of the isometry \(t_a ho_{ heta}\) and can be found geometrically.

Let \(\ell\) pass through the origin and be perpendicular to \(a\). Then, the sector with angle \( heta\) is bisected by \(\ell\) and \(p\) is determined by inserting \(a\) into the sector.

We've completed the proof that all orientation-preserving isometries are either translations or rotations. Next, we show that all orientation-reversing isometries are either glides or a reflection.

To do this, we again change coordinates. The isometry \( ho_{ heta} r\) is a reflection about \(\ell_0\) through the origin. We can rotate coordinates so that \(\ell_0\) becomes the horizontal axis. Then, the reflection becomes the standard reflection \(r\) and \(t_a\) stays a translation in the new coordinate system. Then, \(m = t_a r\) and operates like:

\[ m egin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = t_a egin{bmatrix} x_1 \ - x_2 \end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} x_1 + a \ -x_2 + a \end{bmatrix} \]

This is precisely a glide - a reflection about the line \(\ell = \{x_2 = rac{1}{2} a_2\}\) followed by translation of \(a_1 e_1\). If \(a_1 = 0\), then \(m\) is a reflection. QED.

Corollary 6.2.4

The glide line of the isometry \(t_a ho_{ heta} r\) is parallel to the line of reflection of \( ho_{ heta} r\).

Isometries that fix the origin are orthogonal linear operators. When coordinates are chose, the orthogonal group \(O_2\) becomes a subgroup of the isometry group \(M\). We can also consider the subgroup of \(M\) of isometries which fix a point of the plane other than the origin. How are they related to the orthogonal group?

Proposition 6.2.5

Suppose coordinates in the plane have been chosen so that the orthogonal group \(O_2\) becomes the subgroup of \(M\) of isometries that fix the origin. Then, the group of isometries that fix a point \(p\) of the plane is the conjugate subgroup \(t_p O_2 t_p^{-1}\).

Proof

Is an isometry \(m\) fixes \(p\), then, \(t_p^{-1} m t_p\) fixes the origin. \(t_p^{-1} m t_p o = t_p^{-1} m p = t_p^{-1} p = o\). Conversely, if \(m\) fixes \(o\), then \(t_p m t_p^{-1}\) fixes \(p\).

We can visualize rotation about \(p\) as first translate by \(t_{-p}\) to move \(p\) to \(0\), then rotate about the origin, then translate back to \(p\).

We go back to the homomorphism \(\pi: M o O_2\).

Proposition 6.2.6

Let \(p\) be a point in the plane and \( ho_{ heta, p}\) be a rotation though \( heta\) about \(p\). Then, \(\pi( ho_{ heta, p}) = ho_{ heta}\). Similarly, if \(r_{\ell}\) is a reflection about \(\ell\) or a glide with glide line \(\ell\) that is parallel to the \(x\)-axis, then \(\pi(r_{\ell}) = r\).

Points and Vectors

Generally, there is no convincing reason to distinguish a point \(p\) of the plane \(P\) from the vector which goes from the origin \(o\) to \(p\). When working with isometries, we maintain the distinction. We introduce a copy of the plane, called \(V\), and think of its elements as translation vectors. \(t_v(p) = p + v\), shifting every point of the plane by \(v\).

Suppose we shift coordinates in \(P\) by a translation, \(\eta = t_w\). Then, the rule is that \(\eta(p') = p\) or \(p' + w = p\). An isometry \(m\) changes to \(\eta^{-1} m \eta = t_{-w} m t_w\). Applying this rule with \(m = t_v\), then \(m' = t_{-w} t_v t_w = t_v\). The points of \(P\) get new coordinates but the translation vectors are unchanged.

If we change coordinates by orthogonal operator \(\varphi\), then \(\varphi(p') = p\). If \(m = t_v\), then \(m' = \varphi^{-1} t_v \varphi = t_{ ho^{-1}(v)}\). So \( ho ho^{-1}(v) = v\). The effect of change of coordinates is the same as \(P\) on \(V\). In other words, orthogonal operators act on \(V\) but not on \(P\) unless the origin is chosen.

docs.title: Cyclic, Dihedral Subgroups
docs.text:
Theorem 6.3.1.1: Characterizing Subgroup

Let \(G\) be a finite subgroup of the orthogonal group \(O_2\). There's an integer \(n\) such that \(G\) is one of the following groups.

  • \(C_n\): The cyclic group of order \(n\) generated by the rotation \(\rho_{\theta}\) where \(\theta = 2 \pi / n\).
  • \(D_n\): The dihedral group of order \(2n\) generated by elements \(\rho_{\theta}\) where \(\theta = 2 \pi / n\) and a reflection \(r'\) about a line \(\ell\) through the origin.

Generally, \(n\) is how finely we can rotate around the unit circle. If \(n = 4\), then \(\theta\) corresponds to \(90^{\circ}\). The \(n\) rotations split the circle into \(n\) equal steps. After \(n\) rotations, we return to the start.

We describe the dihedral group \(D_n\) before proving the theorem. We choose coordinates so that \(\ell\) is the horizontal axis so the group simpy contains the standard reflection \(r\) with matrix:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \\ & -1 \end{bmatrix} \]

If we write \(\rho\) for \(\rho_{\theta}\), then the \(2n\) elements of the group are the \(n\) powers of \(\rho^i\) and the \(n\) products \(\rho^i r\). The rule is that:

\[ r \rho = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \\ & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c & -s \\ s & c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c & s \\ -s & c \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \\ & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \rho^{-1} r \]

If we first rotate and then reflect across the horizontal axis, that's equivalent to reflecting across the horizontal axis first and then rotating in the other direction by the same angle.

Let \(x = \rho_{2 \pi / n}\) and \(y = r\). Then,

Proposition 6.3.1.2

The dihedral group \(D_n\) has order \(2n\), generated by elements \(x, y\) that satisfy the relations:

\[ x^n = 1, \ y^2 = 1, \ yx = x^{-1} y \]

The elements of \(D_n\) are:

\[ 1, x, \dots, x^{n - 1}; \ y, xy, x^2y, \dots, x^{n - 1} y \]

With the first two relations, we can re-write the third as:

\[ yx = x^{-1} y \implies xyx = y \implies yxyx = y^2 = 1 \]

or

\[ yx = x^{n - 1}y \]

When \(n = 3\), the relations are the same as \(S_3\).

Corollary 6.3.1.3

The dihedral group \(D_3\) and the symmetric group \(S_3\) are isomorphic.

For \(n \geq 3\), the dihedral and symmetric groups are not isomorphic since \(D_n\) has order \(2n\) and \(S_n\) has order \(n!\).

When \(n \geq 3\), the elements of \(D_n\) are orthogonal operators that take a \(n\) sided polygon to itself, the group of symmetries of \(\Delta\). A regular \(n\)-gon is carried to itself by rotation by \(2 \pi / n\) about its center along with some reflections. The group of symmetries is \(D_n\).

\(D_1\) is the group \(\{1, r\}\) meaning that it is a cyclic group like \(C_2\). However, the element \(r\) of \(D_1\) is a reflection while the non-identity element of \(C_2\) is rotation with angle \(\pi\).

The group \(D_2 = \{1, \rho, r, \rho r\}\) is isomorphic to the Klein four group (look it up!).

A subgroup \(\Gamma\) of the additive group \(\R^+\) is called discrete if there exists some small positive number \(\epsilon\) such that every non zero element \(c \in \Gamma\) has absolute value \(\geq \epsilon\).

Lemma 6.3.1.4

Let \(\Gamma\) be a discrete subgroup of \(\R^+\). Then, either \(\Gamma = \{0\}\) or \(\Gamma\) is the set \(\Z a\) of integer multiples of \(a\).

Proof

\(a, b \in \Gamma \implies a - b \in \Gamma, |a - b| \geq \epsilon\). Therefore, a bounded interval contains a finite number of elements of \(\Gamma\) in it since distinct elements are all separated by \(\epsilon\) and only finitely many elements separated by \(\epsilon\) can fit in the bounded interval.

Suppose \(\Gamma \neq \{0\}\). Then, \(\exists b, -b \neq 0 \in \Gamma\). Let \(a' > 0 \in \Gamma\). We choose the smallest positive element \(a\) since we only need to choose the smallest element of the finite subset of \(\Gamma\) in \(0 \leq x \leq a'\).

We show that \(\Gamma = \Z a\). Since \(a \in \Gamma\), \(\Z a \subset \Gamma\). Let \(b \in \Gamma\), then \(b = ra\) where \(r = m + r_0, m \in \Z, 0 \leq r_0 < 1\). Since \(\Gamma\) is a group, \(b' = b - ma \in \Gamma\), \(b' = r_0 a\). Then, \(0 \leq b' < a\). Since \(a\) is the smallest element in \(\Gamma, b' = 0 \implies b = ma\). Therefore, \(\Gamma \subset \Z a \implies \Gamma = \Z a\).

Finally, we prove the theorem about finite subgroups of \(O_2\).

Proof

Let \(G\) be a finite subgroup of \(O_2\). We want to show that \(G\) is \(C_n\) or \(D_n\). All elements of \(O_2\) are rotations \(\rho_{\theta}\) or reflections \(\rho_{\theta} r\).

  1. Suppose all elements of \(G\) are rotations.

We must show that \(G\) is cyclic. Let \(\Gamma\) be the set of real numbers \(\alpha\) such that \(\rho_{\alpha} \in G\). Then, \(\Gamma\) is a subgroup of \(\R^{+}\) and contains \(2 \pi\). Since \(G\) is finite, \(\Gamma\) is discrete and has the form \(\Z a\). Then, \(G\) consists of integer multiples through \(\alpha\). Since \(2 \pi \in \Gamma\), it's a multiplier of \(\alpha\). Therefore, \(\alpha = 2 \pi / n\) for some \(n\) and \(G = C_n\).

  1. \(G\) contains a reflection.

Adjust coordinates to the standard reflection \(r \in G\). Let \(H\) be the subgroup consisting of rotations in \(G\). We conclude \(H\) is the cyclic group generated by \(\rho_{\theta}\) for \(\theta = 2 \pi / n\). Then, the products \(\rho_{\theta}^{k}, \rho_{\theta}^{k} r\) are in \(G\) so \(G\) contains the dihedral group \(D_n\). We claim \(G = D_n\). Let \(g \in G\). Then, \(g\) is either a rotation or reflection. If \(g\) is a rotation, then \(g \in H \in D_N\). If \(g\) isa reflection, then \(g = \rho_{\theta} r\). Since \(r \in G, gr = \rho_{\alpha} \implies \rho_{\alpha}\) is a power of \(\rho_{\theta} \implies g \in D_n\).

docs.title: Fixed Point
docs.text:
Theorem 6.3.2.1: Fixed Point Theorem

Let \(G\) be a finite group of isometries of the plane. There is a point in the plane \(p\) fixed by every element of \(G\), i.e. for \(g \in G, g(p) = p\).

Proof

Let \(s\) be a point in the plane and \(S = \{g(s) \mid g \in G\}\). Naturally, \(s \in S\) since \(1(s) = s\).

\(S\) is called the orbit of \(s\) for the action of \(G\). Any element of \(G\) simply permutes the orbit \(S\). We will show that every isometry \(g \in G\) sends \(S\) onto itself.

Consider \(s' \in S, h \in G\). We want to show that \(h(s') \in S\). Suppose \(s' = g(s)\). Since \(G\) is a group, \(hg \in G\) and \(hg(s) = h(s') \implies h(s') \in S\).

Since \(G\) is a group of isometries, \(g \in G\) is injective and since we just showed that \(g\) is surjective, each \(g\) provides a bijection (or permutation) from \(S\) to \(S\).

We list \(S = \{s_1, \dots, s_n\}\). The fixed point is the centroied \(p = \frac{1}{n} (s_1 + \dots + s_n)\).

Lemma 6.3.2.2: Isometries Take Centroids to Centroids

Let \(S = \{s_1, \dots, s_n\}\) be a finite set of points in the plane. and \(p\) be its centroid. Let \(m\) be an isometry. Let \(m\) be an isometry, \(m(p) = p'\). Then, \(p'\) is the centroid of the set \(S' = \{m(s_1), \dots, m(s_n)\}\).

Since \(g\) permutes the orbit, it sends \(S\) to \(S\) and \(p\) to \(p\).

Proof

Suppose \(m = t_a\) or \(m = \varphi\). If \(m = t_a\), then:

\[ p' = p + a = \frac{1}{n} ((s_1 + a) + \dots + (s_n + a)) = \frac{1}{n} (t_a(s_1) + \dots + t_a(s_n)) \]

If \(m = \varphi\), then since \(\varphi\) is a linear operator:

\[ p' = \varphi(p) = \varphi \frac{1}{n} (s_1 + \dots + s_n) = \frac{1}{n} (\varphi(s_1) + \dots + \varphi(s_n)) \]

Corollary 6.3.2.3

Let \(G\) be a finite subgroup of \(M\) of isometries of the plane. Then, \(G\) is one of the groups \(C_n\) or \(D_n\).

docs.title: Discrete Isometry Groups
docs.text:
Like a kaleidoscope, the union of group actions on a figure can form an interesting figure. Consider a random figure \(R\). Each element of \(g\) moves \(R\) to some new position \(gR\). The figure \(F = \bigcup_{g \in G} gR\). \(h\) sends to \(gR\) to \(hgR \in F\). If \(R\) is sufficiently random, \(G\) will be the group of symmetries of \(F\).

Some subgroups of \(M\) are too wild to have reasonable geometry.

Definition 6.4.1: Discrete Groups

A group \(G\) of isometries of the plane \(P\) is discrete if it does not contain arbitrarily small translations or rotations. Specifically, \(G\) is discrete is there exists \(\epsilon \in \R_{\geq 0}\) so that:

  • If an element of \(G\) is translation by non-zero vector \(a\), then \(|a| \geq \epsilon\).
  • If an element of \(G\) is the rotation through \(\theta\) about some point in the plane, then \(|\theta| \geq \epsilon\).

Translations and rotations are all of the orientation-preserving isometries. Orientation-reversing isometries are also bounded below - if \(m\) is a glide with nonzero glide vector \(v\), then \(m^2\) is the translation \(t_{2v}\).

docs.title: Fisher Information Matrix
docs.text: The Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) plays an important role in statistics and optimization. In the post, we will review the FIM and it's role in statistics, it's role in designing pre-conditioners for natural gradient optimization methods and how it interacts with singular models.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
We motivate the FIM by considering the following problem. Suppose we have some observed sample \(X_1, X_2, \dots \sim_{\text{i.i.d.}} p(x; \theta)\) where \(\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \R\). Consider an unbiased estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) and suppose we plot the likelihood function over many different possible \(\theta\) candidates.

Consider two scenarios. In one scenario, the likelihood function is sharply peaked while in the other, the likelihood function is flat. Which shape tells you more information about the true parameter?

It seems like the sharply peaked likelihood function intuitively would make it easier to distinguish the true parameter \(\theta_0\) from the rest. How can we quantify this and moreover, how good can we get at distinguishing \(\theta_0\)?

First, let's introduce the score function:

\[ s(\theta) = \nabla_{\theta} \log p(\mathbf{x} ; \theta) \]

This is the derivative of the log-likelihood function. Consider a finite-difference approximation. Suppose in both scenarios, our distribution is peaked around \(\theta'\) and we take some step \(d\theta\) to the right. In the highly peaked scenario, we would observe a large decrease in likelihood while in the flatter scenario, we would observe a much more mild decrease.

So the score would be larger in a more sharply peaked scenario. The Fisher Information is then the expected variance of the score over the dataset.

\[ \mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{X}[s(\theta)^2] = \int s(\theta)^2 p(x \mid \theta) dx \]

We can measure the Fisher information of each parameter. Imagine many log-likelihood curves laid atop one another. At a particular parameter, we can look at the variance of the log-likelihood gradients over all of these curves. The FIM is mathematically, a weighted sum-of-squares of gradients so a larger FIM would mean that a particular parameter is distinguishable from its neighbors.

In the multivariate scenario, the log-likelihood gradient is no longer a singular number but rather a gradient. To square the gradient, we can take it's outer-product. This gives us the Fisher Information Matrix.

\[ \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}[s(\mathbf{\theta}) s(\theta)^T] \]

This plays a role in the Cramer-Rao Lower Bound which lower-bounds the asymptotic variance of any unbiased estimator by the inverted Fisher information matrix (matrix inequality). That particular bound is not the focus of this post though.

docs.title: Hessian Matrix
docs.text:
You might suspect that the FIM could be intuitively related to the Hessian at this point. The Hessian is a matrix of \(2\)nd derivatives while the FIM is the outer-product of gradients. Additionally, the utility of the FIM is essentially to analyze the curvature of the log-likelihood at a specific point which is precisely what the Hessian does! It turns, out they are related.

Consider the Hessian of the log-likelihood. We have:

\[ [H( heta)]_{ij} = rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j} \mathbb{E}_X[\log p(X \mid heta)] \]

The FIM (written as \(F\)) here is:

\[ [F( heta)]_{ij} = \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} \log p(X \mid heta) \cdot rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} \log p(X \mid heta) ight ] \] \[ = \mathbb{E}_{X} [ abla_{ heta_i} \ \log p(x \mid heta) \cdot abla_{ heta_j} \ \log p(x \mid heta)] \]

We will show that:

\[ F( heta) = - \mathbb{E}_{X}[H( heta)] \]

Let's establish some basic tools.

\[ \int_{X} p(x \mid heta) dx = 1 \]

Any normalizable probability distribution must integrate to \(1\). It follows that

\[ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} \int_{X} p(x \mid heta) dx = \int_{X} rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta) dx = 0 \] \[ \int_{X} rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i \partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta) dx = 0 \]

We can also compute the \(2\)nd derivative of the log-likelihood.

\[ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j} \log p(x \mid heta) = rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} \cdot rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \] \[ = rac{[ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)] p(x \mid heta) - rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta) \cdot rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)^2} \] \[ = rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} - rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \cdot rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \]

Now that we have our basic tools, let's compute the expected Hessian. By the linearity of expectation,

\[ \mathbb{E}_{X}[H( heta)]_{ij} = \mathbb{E}_{X} [ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j} \log p(x \mid heta)] = \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} - rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \cdot rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} ight ] \] \[ = \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} ight ] - \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \cdot rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} ight ] \]

The first term evaluates to \(0\) as established beforehand.

\[ \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} ight ] = \int rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} p(x \mid heta) dx \] \[ = \int rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i heta_j}p(x \mid heta) dx = 0 \]

Thus, we have:

\[ \mathbb{E}_{X}[H( heta)]_{ij} = - \mathbb{E}_{X} \left [ rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_j} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} \cdot rac{ rac{\partial}{\partial heta_i} p(x \mid heta)}{p(x \mid heta)} ight ] = - \mathbb{E}_{X} [ abla_{ heta_i} \ \log p(x \mid heta) \cdot abla_{ heta_j} \ \log p(x \mid heta)] \] \[ = - F( heta) \]

Hence,

\[ F( heta) = - \mathbb{E}_X[H( heta)] \]

This equality only works because we're integrating over \(X\) using the density \(p(x \mid heta)\). In other words, the FIM coincides with the negative expected Hessian when both expectations are being taken over \(p(x \mid heta)\). Typically, the expected Hessian of the loss is taken over data while we compute the FIM of our model which are normally different.

We should also draw a subtle distinction. The FIM measures sensitivity of the model's output distribution, \(p(y \mid x_n, heta)\) w.r.t. the model parameters. The empirical Fisher instead uses labels \(y_n\) from the dataset. There has been research1 showing2 that the empirical Fisher does not make for a particularly good pre-conditioner.

docs.title: QR Decomposition
docs.text:
We introduce the tools used in QR-decomposition - outer-products, projectors, and the product of Householder reflectors. These tools are frequently used to compute QR decompositions so we can review this problem as well.

We specifically review choice chapters from the QR-decomposition section of Trefethen & Bau.

docs.title: Projectors
docs.text:
Definition 1.1: Projector

A projector is a square matrix that satisfies

\[ P^2 = P \]

\(P\) is also called idempotent. This definition includes both orthogonal and non-orthogonal projectors. Non-orthogonal projectors may be called oblique projectors.

As suggested by its name, a projector takes a vector \(v\) and projects it onto a certain subspace (kind of like the shadow casted by \(v\) on \(\text{span}(P)\)). Once we have projected \(v\) onto \(\text{span}(P)\), a secondary projection ought to do nothing, which is why we require that \(P^2 = P\). Mathematically,

Suppose \(v = Px\). Then,

\[ Pv = P(Px) = P^2x = Px = v \]

Naturally, \(Pv - v \in \text{Ker}(P)\). This is precisely the component of \(v\) which is discarded by the projection.

docs.title: Complementary Projector
docs.text:
If \(P\) is a projector, then \(I - P\) is also a projector.

\[ (I - P)^2 = I - 2P + P^2 = I - P \]

\(I - P\) projects on the null-space of \(P\). We have that:

Theorem 1.1.1: Image(I - P) = Kernel(P)

Proof

Suppose \(v \in \text{Ker}(P), v \neq 0\). Then, \(Pv = 0\) and \((I - P)v = v - Pv = v - 0 = v\) so \(v \in \text{Image}(I - P)\). Therefore, \(\text{Ker}(P) \subseteq \text{Image}(I - P)\).

Suppose \(v \in \text{Image}(I - P)\). Then, \((I - P)v = v - Pv\). However, we know that \(P\) maps \(v - Pv\) to \(0\) so \(\text{Image}(I - P) \subseteq \text{Ker}(P)\) (the two spaces are comparable because \(P\) is square).

Therefore, \(\text{Image}(I - P) = \text{Ker}(P)\).

Without too much effort, we can show that \(\text{Ker}(I - P) = \text{Image}(P)\) as well and that \(\text{Image}(P) \bigcap \text{Ker}(P) = \{0\}\).

In short, a projector separates the vector space into two subspaces. Let \(S_1, S_2\) be subspaces of \(\mathbb{C}^m\) such that \(S_1 \bigcap S_2 = \{0\}\) and \(\mathbb{C}^m = S_1 \oplus S_2\) (each vector in \(\mathbb{C}^m\) can be uniquely expressed as a sum of \(s_1 \in S_1\) and \(s_2 \in S_2\)). The pair \((S_1, S_2)\) is called complementary subspaces. There is a projector \(P\) such that \(\text{Image}(P) = S_1, \text{Ker}(P) = S_2\). We say that \(P\) is a projector onto \(S_1\) along \(S_2\).

An application: Given \(x \in \mathbb{C}^m\), what's the component of \(x\) in the direction of a particular eigenvector \(v\) of a matrix \(A\) (which holds a complete set of eigenvectors)? The answer is \(Px\) where \(P\) is a particular rank-one projector.

Note that if \(P\) is a rank \(k\) projector, \(I - P\) is a rank \(n - k\) projector where \(n\) is the number of rows / columns in \(P\).

docs.title: Orthogonal Projector
docs.text:
Definition 1.2.1: Orthogonal Projector

An orthogonal projector is one which projects onto a subspace \(S_1\) along \(S_2\) where \(S_1, S_2\) are orthogonal.

Orthogonal projectors don't need to be orthogonal matrices.

Theorem 1.2.2: Orthogonal Projectors are Symmetric

Proof

Let \(P\) be an orthogonal projector. We have that

\[ \text{Image}(P) \perp \text{Ker}(P) \]

and

\[ \text{Image}(P) \perp \text{Image}(I - P) \]

Suppose \(Px_1 \neq 0, (I - P)x_2 \neq 0\). Then by orthogonality,

\[ (P x_1)^T ((I - P) x_2) = 0 \] \[ x_1^T P^T (I - P) x_2 = 0 \] \[ x_1^T P^T x_2 - x_1^T P^T P x_2 = 0 \] \[ x_1^T P^T x_2 = x_1^T P^T P x_2 \implies P^T = P^T P \] \[ (P^T)^T = P = P^T \]

Therefore, orthogonality of the projected subspaces implies that the orthogonal projector must be symmetric.

A particularly important kind of orthogonal projector is the rank-one orthogonal projector,

\[ P_q = qq^T \]

The complement is the rank \(m - 1\) orthogonal projector which removes the component in the direction of \(q\),

\[ P_{\perp q} = I - qq^T \]

For idempotency, it is assumed that \(q\) has norm \(1\). However, normalizing is not hard.

docs.title: QR Factorization
docs.text:
The goal of QR factorization is to construct a sequence of orthonormal matrices \(q_1, q_2, \dots\) that spans the successive column spaces of some matrix \(A\). More precisely, for \(A \in \mathbb{C}^{m \times n}, m \geq n\), we want:

\[ \text{Span}(q_1, \dots, q_j) = \text{Span}(a_1, \dots, a_j) \]

for \(j = 1, \dots, n\). This amounts to the condition that:

\[ \left[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_n \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} q_1 & q_2 & \cdots & q_n \end{array}\right] \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} & \cdots & r_{1n} \\ & r_{22} & & \vdots \\ & & \ddots & \\ & & & r_{nn} \end{bmatrix} \]

The coefficients in \(R\) express that a column \(a_j\) can be represented as a linear combination \(\sum_{i = 1}^j r_{ij} q_i\) of the orthonormal columns of \(Q\). More generally, we have \(A = QR\) where \(Q\) is a \(m \times n\) matrix with orthonormal columns and \(R\) is a \(n \times n\) upper-triangular matrix. This factorization is called the reduced \(QR\) factorization of \(A\).

docs.title: Gram-Schmidt
docs.text:
Orthogonalization can be achieved by removing components of past \(q\)'s and then normalizing. First, orthogonalization can be done like so:

\[ v_j = a_j - (q_1^T a_j) q_1 - (q_2^T a_j) q_2 - \dots - (q_{j - 1}^T a_j) q_{j - 1} \]

Thus, to explicitly construct the \(q\) vectors is to solve for \(q_j\) from the sum \(a_j = \sum_{i = 1}^j r_{ij} q_i\). Specifically,

\[ q_1 = \frac{a_1}{r_{11}} \] \[ q_2 = \frac{a_2 - r_{12} q_2}{r_{22}} \] \[ q_j = \frac{a_j - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} r_{ij} q_j}{r_{jj}} \]

This naturally produces a sequence of orthonormal vectors as it's removing the component of the previous \(q\)'s in the current \(a\) and it's normalizing. Naturally, we have that \(r_{ij} = q_i^T a_j\) and \(|r_{jj}| = ||a_j - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} r_{ij} q_i||_2\).

It can be shown that a unique QR factorization exists for each full rank matrix \(A\).

Code:

def gram_schmidt(A: np.ndarray):
    n = A.shape[1]
    q = np.zeros_like(A)
    r = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=float)

    for i in range(n):
        components = np.zeros_like(A[:, i])
        a_i = A[:, i]
        for j in range(i):
            r_ij = a_i @ q[:, j].T
            r[j, i] = r_ij
            components += r_ij * q[:, j]

        diff = a_i - components
        norm = np.linalg.norm(diff)
        q[:, i] = diff / norm
        r[i, i] = norm

    return q, r

docs.title: Modified Gram-Schmidt
docs.text:
Interestingly, we can also do Gram-Schmidt via projectors.

\[ q_1 = \frac{P_1 a_1}{||P_1 a_1||}, q_2 = \frac{P_2 a_2}{||P_2 a_2||}, \dots, q_n = \frac{P_n a_n}{||P_n a_n||}, \]

\(P_j\) is the orthogonal projector along \(\text{Span}(q_1, \dots, q_{j - 1})\) where \(P_{j = 1} = I\). We can represent it explicitly. Suppose \(\hat{Q}_{j - 1} = [q_1 | q_2 | \dots | q_{j - 1}]\). Then,

\[ P_j = I - \hat{Q}_{j - 1} \hat{Q}_{j - 1}^T \]

Naturally, we can re-write: $$ P_j = I - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} q_i \otimes q_i = I - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} q_i q_i^T $$

Then, $$ P_j a_j = (I - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} q_i q_i^T) a_j = a_j - \sum_{i = 1}^{j - 1} (q_i^T a_j) q_i $$ which is precisely the equation for \(v_j\).

The standard (numerically unstable) Gram-Schmidt algorithm computes a single orthogonal projection at a time, \(v_j = P_j a_j\). It's intuitively clear that

\[ P_j = P_{\perp q_{j - 1}} \dots P_{\perp q_1} \] \[ v_j = \left ( \prod_{i = 1}^{j - 1} P_{\perp q_{i}} \right ) a_j \]

This suggests an alternative, iterative way of computing Gram-Schmidt.

\[v_j^{(1)} = a_j\] \[v_j^{(2)} = P_{\perp q_i} v_j^{(1)} = v_j^{(1)} - (q_1^T v_j^{(1)}) q_1\]

Generally, \(v_j^{(i)} = P_{\perp q_{i - 1}} v_j^{(i - 1)}\). We can observe that this is equivalent to the standard Gram-Schmidt except that it builds the orthonormal vectors iteratively rather than sequentially.

The matrix form can also be written via triangular orthogonalization.

Consider \([a_1 | \dots | a_n]\). The \(i\)'th step of matrix GS normalizes the \(i\)'th column as \(v_i = a_i / r_{ii}\) and subtracts \(\frac{r_{ij}}{r_ii} a_i\) from the "future" columns \(j > i\). This is the opposite order from standard GS - "future" columns are orthogonalized from the current column. This too can be represented as a triangular matrix. In the first step, we have:

\[ [a_1 | \dots | a_n] \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{r_{11}} & - \dfrac{r_{12}}{r_{11}} & - \dfrac{r_{13}}{r_{11}} & \dots \\ & 1 & & \\ & & 1 & \\ & & & \ddots \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} q_1 | v_2^{(2)} | \dots | v_n^{(2)} \end{bmatrix} \]

On iteration \(j\), column \(i\) of the output matrix is (where \(j < i < n\)):

\[ v_i^{(j)} = v_i^{(j - 1)} - r_{ji} q_j = v_i^{(j - 1)} - \frac{r_{ji}}{r_{jj}} v_j^{(j)} \]

We have:

\[ R_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & & & \\ & \dfrac{1}{r_{22}} & \dfrac{-r_{23}}{r_{22}} & \cdots \\ & & 1 & \\ & & & \ddots \end{bmatrix} \] \[ R_j = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & & & & & \\ & \ddots & & & & \\ & & \dfrac{1}{r_{jj}} & \dfrac{-r_{j,j+1}}{r_{jj}} & \cdots & \dfrac{-r_{jn}}{r_{jj}} \\ & & & 1 & & \\ & & & & \ddots & \\ & & & & & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

At the end, we have \(A R_1 R_2 \dots R_n = \hat{Q}\).

Code:

def modified_gram_schmidt(A: np.ndarray):
    n = A.shape[1]
    v = A.copy()
    q = np.zeros_like(A)
    r = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=float)

    for i in range(n):
        r[i, i] = np.linalg.norm(v[:, i])
        q[:, i] = v[:, i] / r[i, i]

        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            r[i, j] = q[:, i] @ v[:, j]
            v[:, j] -= r[i, j] * q[:, i]

    return q, r

docs.title: Householder Triangularization
docs.text:
While Gram-Schmidt iteration applies successive triangular matrices to build:

\[ A R_1 R_2 \dots R_n = \hat{Q} \]

where \(R^{-1} = R_1 R_2 \dots R_N\), the product \(\hat{R} = R_n^{-1} \dots R_2^{-1} R_1^{-1}\) is upper triangular and \(A = \hat{Q} \hat{R}\) produces a reduced QR factorization of \(A\).

The Householder method applies successive unitary matrices \(Q_k\) to the left of \(A\) to produces the upper triangular matrix \(R\).

\[ Q_n \dots Q_2 Q_1 A = R \]

where \(Q^* = Q_n \dots Q_2 Q_1\) and the product \(Q = Q_1^* Q_2^* \dots Q_n^*\) is unitary so \(A = QR\) is a full QR factorization of \(A\).

Thus Gram-Schmidt can be thought of as triangular orthogonalization while Householder is orthogonal triangularization.

Definition 2.3.1: Householder Matrix

Let \(v \in \R^m\). An \(m \times m\) matrix \(H\) of the form:

\[ H = I - \beta vv^T, \beta = \frac{2}{v^T v} \]

is a Householder reflection and \(v\) is the Householder vector.

Multiplying a vector \(x\) by \(H\) reflects \(x\) about \(\text{Span}(v)^{\perp}\). Basically, if \(\beta\) had a \(1\) in its numerator, then \(H\) would send the \(v\)-component of vectors to \(0\) (\(\text{Image}(H) = \text{Span}(v)^{\perp}\)). Since \(\beta\) has a \(2\), it doubles the subtraction and ends up reflecting about \(\text{Span}(v)^{\perp}\).

Courtesty of MMIDS textbook & Claude:

Theorem 2.3.2: Householder reflections are orthogonal matrices

Proof

Let \(H = I - 2 \frac{vv^T}{v^T v}\). Let \(a = \frac{vv^T}{v^T v}\) so \(a^T = a\).

\[ H^T H = (I - 2a)^T (I - 2a) = (I - 2a) (I - 2a) = I + 4a - 4 a^T a = I + 4a - 4a = I \]

Hence \(H\) is orthogonal.

Like we stated earlier, one way to compute a QR-decomposition is to find a sequence of orthogonal matrices \(H_1, \dots, H_m\) that triangularize \(A\):

\[ H_m \dots H_2 H_1 A = R \]

Then,

\[ A = H_1^T H_2^T \dots H_m^T H_m \dots H_2 H_1 A = H_1^T H_2^T \dots H_m^T R \]

so \(Q = H_1^T H_2^T \dots H_M^T\) is also orthogonal as it is a product of orthogonal matrices.

With a carefully chosen Householder vector, we can introduce \(0\)'s into \(A\), thus iteratively triangularizing it. Set

\[ v_1 =||a_1|| e_1 - a_1 \] \[ H_1 = I - 2 \frac{v_1 v_1^T}{v_1^T v_1} \]

Drop the index. Call \(||a_1|| = c \implies v = c e_1 - a_1\) where \(e_1\) is the unit vector and \(e_1^T a_1 = a_{11}\). Then,

\[ v^T a_1 = c e_1^T a_1 - a_1^T a_1 = c a_{11} - c^2 = -c (c - a_{11}) \] \[ v^T v = (c e_1 - a_1)^T (c e_1 - a_1) = c^2 - 2 c a_1^T e_1 + a_1^T a_1 \] \[ = c^2 - 2 c a_{11} + c^2 = 2c^2 - 2 c a{11} = 2c (c - a_{11}) \]

So:

\[ H_1 a_1 = a_1 - 2 v \frac{v^T a_1}{v^T v} = a_1 - 2 v \frac{-c (c - a_{11})}{2c (c - a_{11})} \] \[ = a_1 + v \implies H_1 a_1 = ||a_1|| e_1 \]

The first row of \(H_1\) is \(q_1\). Since \(H_1\) is an orthogonal projector, \(\text{Row One}(H_1) = H_1 e_1\). We have that \(H_1 a_1 = ||a_1|| e_1\). Apply it again to get \(H_1 (||a_1|| e_1) = ||a_1|| H_1 e_1 = a_1 \implies H_1 e_1 = \dfrac{a_1}{||a_1||} = q_1^T\). Therefore, the \(j\)'th element in the first row of \(H_1 A\) is \(q_1^T a_j\) which is precisely what we want in \(R\).

The goal for successive Householder reflectors is to leave the first few rows alone and only affect subsequent rows. Generally, we want:

\[ H_k = \begin{bmatrix} I_{k - 1 \times k -1} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} & F_k \end{bmatrix} \]

where \(F_k = I_{(n - k + 1) \times (n - k + 1)} - 2 \dfrac{v_k v_k^T}{v_k^T v_k}\), \(v_k = ||a_k|| e_{n - k + 1} - a_k\). The action is to preserve the existing rows (applying the identity matrix to them) while completing the \(k\)'th row of \(R\).

This amounts to a sequential change of basis.

Code:

def householder_explicit(A: np.ndarray):
    m, n = A.shape
    W = A.astype(float)

    Q = np.eye(m)

    for k in range(min(n, m - 1)):
        x = W[k:, k]
        x_norm = np.linalg.norm(x)
        if x_norm == 0.0:
            continue

        v = x.copy()
        v[0] += np.sign(x[0]) * x_norm
        v /= np.linalg.norm(v)

        H_k = np.eye(m)
        H_k[k:, k:] -= 2.0 * np.outer(v, v)

        W = H_k @ W
        Q = Q @ H_k

    R = np.triu(W)

    return Q, R

docs.text: Finally, we review outer-products.

docs.title: Outer Products
docs.text:
Theorem 3.1.1:

Matrix multiplication can be expressed as a sum of outer products.

Proof

Consider the generic \(AB\) matrix multiplication.

\[ AB = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & \dots & a_{1N} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{M1} & \dots & a_{MN} \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} b_{11} & \dots & b_{1P} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ b_{N1} & \dots & b_{NP} \\ \end{bmatrix} = C \] \[ c_{kl} = \sum_{i = 1}^N a_{ki} b_{il} \]

The outer-product of two vectors is defined as:

\[ a_i \otimes b_j = ab^T = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_N \end{bmatrix} \otimes \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ \vdots \\ b_M \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 b_1 & \dots & a_1 b_M \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_N b_1 & \dots & a_N b_M \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

Let \(C' = a_i \otimes b_j\). Then, \(C'_{kl} = a_k b_l\).

Generally, we can express:

\[ AB = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 | \dots | a_N \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} & b_1 & \\ \hline & \vdots & \\ \hline & b_N & \end{bmatrix} = C = \sum_{i = 1}^N a_i \otimes b_i^T \]

In other words, a matrix-multiply can be expressed as a sum of rank-one outer-products. To see this, observe that:

\[ C_{kl} = [\sum_{i = 1}^N a_i \otimes b_i^T]_{kl} \] \[ = \sum_{i = 1}^N (a_i \otimes b_i^T)_{kl} \] \[ = \sum_{i = 1}^N a_{ki} b_{il} \]

This is identical to the element-wise formula given by the regular process for matrix multiplication and holds for generic indices.

docs.title: Two Fundamental Subspaces
docs.text:
It's quite easy to identify two subspaces - the kernel or null-space and the image. These subspaces are both defined by a linear map.

Consider a linear map \(L: X \to Y\). Then,

\[ \text{Ker}(L) = \{x \in X \mid L(x) = 0\} \] \[ \text{Im}(L) = \{L(x) : x \in X\} \subset Y \]

The kernel is the subspace of vectors in the domain which are sent to \(0\) and the image is the subspace of vectors in \(Y\) which "came from" \(X\). From this, we can recover Rank-Nullity, etc.

The image in particular is also called the span or column-space of \(A\). But why is it called the column-space?

docs.title: Linear Maps, Column Space
docs.text:
Let \(x_1, x_2, x \in X\) and \(s \in \mathbb{F}\) where \(\mathbb{F}\) is some field (like \(\mathbb{C}, \R\)). Then, \(L: X \to Y\) is a linear map iff

\[ L(x_1 + x_2) = L(x_1) + L(x_2) \] \[ L(sx) = sL(x) \]

This is still just an abstract map. Now suppose \(X, Y\) are finite-dimensional. Fix a basis \(\{e_1, \dots, e_n\}\) for \(X\) and \(\{f_1, \dots, f_m\}\) for \(Y\). Then, any vector \(x \in X\) can be represented as:

\[ x = \sum_{i = 1}^n s_i e_i = [e_1 \dots e_n] \begin{bmatrix} s_1 \\ \vdots \\ s_n \end{bmatrix} \]

Then,

\[ L(x) = L([e_1 \dots e_n] \begin{bmatrix} s_1 \\ \vdots \\ s_n \end{bmatrix} ) \] \[ = L([e_1 \dots e_n]) \begin{bmatrix} s_1 \\ \vdots \\ s_n \end{bmatrix} \]

When we apply \(L\) to each basis vector \(e_i\), the output vector can be represented as a linear combination of the output basis vectors. Specifically,

\[ L(e_j) = f_1 A_{1j} + \dots + f_m A_{mj} = \sum_i A_{ij} f_i \]

This choice of which dimension to contract over is pure convention.

So we have:

\[ L(x) = \begin{bmatrix}f_1 A_{11} + \dots + f_m A_{m1} & \dots & f_1 A_{1n} + \dots + f_m A_{mn}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} s_1 \\ \vdots \\ s_n \end{bmatrix} \] \[ = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 & \dots & f_m \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & \dots & A_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ A_{m1} & \dots & A_{mn} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} s_1 \\ \vdots \\ s_n \end{bmatrix} \] \[ = F A s \]

When we write a vector like \([1, 2, 3]^T\), we are really writing down \(s\) as the coordinate representation within a specific basis. Additionally, in most cases, \(F\) as a collection of basis vectors in \(Y\) is just the identity matrix (typically if we are taking an orthonormal basis in \(F\)) so this really reduces to:

\[ L(v) = As \]

Each column of a matrix merely encodes the action of the linear operator on a basis vector in the domain. Hence why it is appropriate to call this a "column-space". We also recover the typical formula of matrix-multiplication. Computationally, we are taking inner-products between the rows of \(A\) and the vector \(s\) but this is equivalent to scaling each column by the corresponding element of \(s\). Write \(A = [A_1 | \dots | A_n]\). If we ignore \(F\) as the identity, then \(L(s)\) (where \(s\) is the coordinate vector) is:

\[ L(s) = L(\sum_i s_i e_i) = \sum_i s_i A_i \]

docs.title: Orthogonal Complements
docs.text:
Given a subspace \(E \subset V\), define the orthogonal complement of \(E\) in \(V\) as:

\[ E^{\perp} = \{v \in V: \forall e \in E, \langle e, v \rangle = 0\} \]

This is the collection of vectors which are orthogonal to every vector in \(E\). Hence why it is the complement.

(For convenience, we will now speak about linear maps and their matrix representation semi-interchangeably).

Now, recall the adjoint of a linear map \(L^*\) is defined as:

\[ \langle L(x), y \rangle = \langle x, L^*(y) \rangle \] \[ (Ax)^T y = x^T A^T y \]

Theorem 3.1: Orthogonality and Kernel

\[ \text{Ker}(L^*) = \text{Img}(L)^{\perp} \]

Here, \(L\) and \(L^*\) can be swapped and perpendicularity is symmetric.

Proof

Suppose \(w \in \text{Ker}(L^*)\). Then,

\[ L^* (w) = 0 \iff \forall v \in V, \langle v, L^*w \rangle = 0 \] \[ \iff \forall v \in V, \langle L(v), w \rangle = 0 \] \[ \iff w \in \text{Img}(L)^{\perp} \]

Now view the matrix-vector product by taking inner-products between rows and \(s\). Specifically,

\[ Ax = \begin{bmatrix} A_{1, :}^T x \\ \vdots \\ A_{m, :}^T x \end{bmatrix} \]

Observe that this is \(0\) iff \(x\) is orthogonal to every row of \(A\). But each row of \(A\) is also a column of \(A^T\).

Suppose \(Ax = 0\). Then, \(x \in \text{Ker}(A)\). But this also means \(x\) is orthogonal to each column of \(A^T\). Since \(\text{Img}(A^T)\) is the space of all linear combinations and the inner-product is bilinear, it follows that \(x\) is in the orthogonal complement of \(\text{Img}(A^T)\).

So we get that:

\[ \text{Ker}(A) = \text{Img}(A^T)^{\perp} \]

docs.title: Orthogonal Projections
docs.text:
Finally, we will prove that orthogonal projections minimize the distance to a subspace. First,

Definition 4.1: Orthogonal Projection

An orthogonal projection is a projection where the kernel and image are orthogonal subspaces.

\[ P_E: E^{\perp} \oplus E \to E \] \[ P_{E^{\perp}}: E^{\perp} \oplus E \to E^{\perp} \]

Theorem 4.2: Orthogonal Projection Minimizes Distance

For each \(v \in E \oplus E^{\perp}\) and \(w \in E\), the distance from \(v\) to \(e\) is minimized if \(w = P_E(v)\) i.e.

\[ |v - w| \geq |v - P_E(v)| \]

equality is clearly achieved when \(w = P_E(v)\).

Proof

Let \(v = v_1 + v_2, v_1 = P_E(v), v_2 = v - P_E(v) \in E^{\perp}\). For any \(w \in E\),

\[ |v - w|^2 = |v_1 + v_2 - w|^2 \] \[ = \langle v_1 + v_2 - w, v_1 + v_2 - w \rangle \] \[ = \langle v_1 - w, v_1 - w \rangle + \langle v_2, v_2 \rangle + \langle v_1 - w, v_2 \rangle + \langle v_2, v_1 - w \rangle \] \[ = |v_1 - w|^2 + |v_2|^2 \] \[ = |v_1 - w|^2 + |v - v_1|^2 \geq |v - v_1|^2 \]

This is basically just Pythagoras. If we have some point above a subspace and we want to find some point which is closest to it, the distance can be computed by Pythagoras. The vertical drop is unavoidable but the horizontal drop is, hence why the smallest error is achieved when the target and error vectors are orthogonal to one another.

docs.title: Linear Regression
docs.text:
Consider the following modeling problem. We have a vector of targets \(y\), a matrix \(X\) where each row represents a single datapoint (and columns are features). We want to find \(\beta\) such that \(X \beta\) is "closest" to \(y\).

There are several approaches to this involving matrix calculus but with those approaches, it's quite hard to remember the exact convention being used for gradients.

Instead, define the error vector

\[ e = y - X \beta \]

Minimizing this error occurs when \(e\) is in \(\text{Img}(X)^{\perp}\). Therefore, \(e \in \text{Ker}(X^T)\). So we have:

\[ X^T e = 0 \] \[ X^T (y - X \beta) = 0 \] \[ X^T X \beta = X^T y \] \[ \beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y \]

This is the simplest and most elegant way I know of to get the standard linear regression equation. More generally, the kernel and image of \(L\) and \(L^*\) have been frequently discussed as the "four fundamental subspaces" but I only just intuited the orthogonal complement (even though in retrospect, it was an incredibly natural idea?) and the connection between orthogonal rows and kernel of the transpose. I wanted to write this up as a nice motivator for the matrix-vector product "formula" which becomes retroactively defined by linearity + a basis.

docs.title: 01 - Itô Integral
docs.text:
Consider a gambling sequence - at each step, toss a fair coin. For \(i = 1, 2, \dots\), let \(\Delta W_i\) be the outcome of the \(i\)'th toss where

\[ \Delta W_i \sim_{\text{i.i.d.}} P(\Delta W_i = \pm 1) = \frac{1}{2} \]

Before each coin toss, place a stake \(X_{i - 1}\). If \(\Delta W_i = 1\), you win \(X_{i - 1}\) and if \(\Delta W_i = -1\), you lose \(X_{i - 1}\).

The gambler's wealth after \(n\) steps is

\[ Y_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n X_{i - 1} \Delta W_i \]

This is basically the Itô Integral in the discrete form. The goal is to define stochastic integrals in continuous time:

\[ Y_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n X_{i - 1} \Delta W_i \rightsquigarrow Y_t = \int_{0}^t X_s dW_s \]

We identify the assumption non-anticipation. \(X_{i - 1}\) cannot rely on future outcomes \(\Delta W_{j > i}\).

docs.title: Random Walk
docs.text:
In the discrete setting, the process \(W\) is called a random walk.

Definition 1.1: Symmetric Simple Random Walk

We define the symmetric simple walk \(\{W_n\}_{n = 0, 1, 2, \dots}\) as

\[ W_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n \Delta W_i, n = 1, 2, \dots; W_0 = 0 \]

Here, \(\Delta W_i\) carries the same meaning as defined in the previous section (hence why the walk is symmetric). We can immediately identify that

  • \(\mathbb{E}[W_n] = 0\) (by linearity of expectation).

  • The variance of \(\Delta W_i\) is \(1\) (this is Rademacher, not Bernoulli) and by additivity of variance under independence, \(\text{Var}(W_i) = n \text{Var}(\Delta W_i) = n\).

  • Since \(W_n\) is a sum of i.i.d. random variables, \(W_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, n)\) by CLT.

With these observations, we can construct a continuous analogue.

docs.title: Brownian Motion
docs.text:
This is a continuous time stochastic process taking continuous values, a limit of the random walk.

Definition 2.1: Brownian Motion

The standard Brownian motionn (Wiener process) is a continuous-time real-valued stochastic process \(\{W_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) with the following properties:

  • \(W_0 = 0\).

  • \(\{W_t\}\) has continuous sample path with probability one - the trajectories are almost always continuous.

  • \(\{W_t\}\) has stationary, normally distributed increments. For \(0 \leq s < t\),

\[ W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t - s) \]
  • \(\{W_t\}\) has independent increments. Increments on non-overlapping time intervals are statistically independent.

From this definition, we can show (informally) that Brownian motion is nowhere differentiable.

\[ \frac{\Delta W_t}{\Delta t} = \frac{W_{t + \Delta t} - W_t}{\Delta t} \sim \frac{1}{\Delta t} \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t) = \mathcal{N}(0, \frac{1}{\Delta t}) \]

In the limit as \(\Delta t \to 0\), the variance explodes. We say that in an \(L^2\) sense, the derivative of Brownian motion does not exist. This non-differentiability requires a new calculus including a new chain rule, a new product rule, etc.

docs.title: Itô Integral
docs.text:
Definition 3.1: Itô Integral

For \(i = 0, 1, \dots, n\), let \(t_i = i \Delta t = \frac{i t}{n}\).

\[ \int_{0}^t X_s dW_s := \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n X_{t_{i - 1}} (W_{t_i} - W_{t_{i - 1}}) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n X_{i - 1} \Delta W_i \]

We divide the time interval \([0, t]\) into \(n\) sub-intervals each with length \(\Delta t\). Looking at the summand on the middle term, \(X\) is evaluated at the left endpoint of the current interval \(X_{t_{i - 1}}\) and is multiplied against the increment of the Brownian motion in that period. This is like approximating an integral using the left Riemann sum.

Here, the limit (and stochastic convergence) are in reference to \(L^2\) convergence.

Definition 3.2: Mean Square Convergence

A sequence \((\xi_n)\) of RVs is said to convergence to an rv \(\xi\) in mean square if for all \(N\), \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_n]^2 < \infty, \mathbb{E}[\xi]^2 < \infty\) and

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[(\xi_n - \xi)^2] = 0 \]

docs.title: Integrals
docs.text:
Example 4.1: Constant Function

Let

\[ Y_t = \int_{0}^t f(s) dW_s = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n f_{i - 1} \Delta W_i \]

where \(f(s)\) only depends on time. Specifically, suppose \(f(s) = c\) is a constant function. Then, we get:

\[ Y_t = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n c \Delta W_i \] \[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n c (W_{t_{i}} - W_{t_{i - 1}}) \]

This is a telescoping sum and we end up with

\[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} c (W_{t_n} - W_0) \] \[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} c W_{t_n} = c W_t \]

Generally, if \(f\) is not constant, \(Y_t\) will not have a closed-form formula. Still, \(Y_t\) is a Gaussian RV with \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0\) (by linearity of expectation=) with variance:

\[ \text{Var}(Y_t) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} f_{i - 1}^2 \text{Var}(\Delta W_i) \] \[ = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} f_{i - 1}^2 \Delta t = \int_{0}^t f^2(s) ds \]

The variance of \(\Delta W_i\) is \(\Delta t\) by the stationary increment property.

docs.title: 02 - New Calculus
docs.text:
Recall that Brownian motion is a continuous time stochastic process with the following properties:

  • \(W_0 = 0\)
  • \(t \mapsto W_t\) w.p.\(1\). (almost surely continuous sample paths)
  • \(W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t - s)\) for \(0 \leq s < t\).
  • Independent increments (non-overlapping time intervals) are statistically independent.

We also defined the Itô Integral as

\[ \int_{0}^t X_s dW_s = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n X_{i - 1} \Delta W_i \]

The integrand is evaluated at the left end-point of each infinitesimal interval (meeting our non-anticipation assumption).

However, what happens if \(X_s\) itself is a random process (as opposed to a constant function)?

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Consider:

\[ \int_0^t W_s dW_s = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^n W_{i - 1} \Delta W_i = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n \]

First, recall that \(\Delta W_i = W_i - W_{i - 1}\). Consider:

\[ W_{i}^2 = (\Delta W_i + W_{i - 1})^2 = \Delta W_i^2 + 2 W_{i - 1} \Delta W_i + W_{i - 1}^2 \]

Then, we can isolate

\[ W_{i - 1} \Delta W_i = \frac{1}{2} [W_{i}^2 - W_{i - 1}^2 - \Delta W_i^2] \]

Then, our integral becomes:

\[ S_n = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^n (W_i^2 - W_{i - 1}^2) - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^n \Delta W_i^2 \]

The first sum telescopes to \(W_n^2 - W_0^2 = W_t^2\). But what about \(Q_n := \sum_{i = 1}^n \Delta W_i^2\)?

Recall that

\[ \Delta W_i \sim_{i.i.d.} \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t) \]

So \(Q_n\) is the sum of squared Gaussian i.i.d. RVs. This is the chi-squared distribution.

\[ Q_n = \sum_{i = 1}^n \Delta W_i^2 \sim \Delta t \cdot \chi^2(n) \]

Two properties of the Chi-squared distribution are that \(\mathbb{E}[\chi_n^2] = n\) and \(\text{Var}(\chi_n^2) = 2n\). So we can recover that:

\[ \mathbb{E}[Q_n] = n \Delta t = t \text{ since $n$ is the number of total time increments} \] \[ \text{Var}(Q_n) = 2n \Delta t^2 = 2 t \Delta t \]

As \(n \to \infty\), we can see that \(\mathbb{E}[Q_n]\) doesn't depend on \(n\) but since \(n\) controls the size of \(\Delta t\), \(\Delta t \to 0\) and the mean-square limit of \(Q_n\) is \(t\).

(Recall that mean square limit of a sequence of random variables is a RV such that the expected square difference with the sequence goes to \(0\) as the sequence grows)

In short, the first sum is $ \frac{1}{2} W_t^2$ and the 2nd sum converges to \(\frac{1}{2} t\).

By the definition of Ito integrals,

\[ \int_0^2 W_s dW_s = \frac{1}{2} W_t^2 - \frac{1}{2} t \]

This is not regular calculus - naive integration produces the first term but not the 2nd!

Doing a left Riemann sum as an approximation to an integral produces an error on the order of \(O(\Delta x)\) which tends to \(0\) as the partition grows finer. The proof for why the \(2\)nd order terms go to \(0\) involve both the mean-value theorem and the extreme value theorem which assume continuity and bounds the derivative. However, Brownian motion is non-differentiable! That's why sample paths are so jagged and why we need a new calculus.

docs.title: Another View
docs.text:
Another reason why \(\int_0^t W_s dW_s = \frac{1}{2} W_t^2 - \frac{1}{2} t\) is that \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0\). We will show this but recall that Since \(X_i\) is non-anticipatory, it contains zero information about \(\Delta W_{i + 1}\) (and hence they are orthogonal). \(Y_t\) is called a martingale or a fair game.

Heuristically,

\[ \mathbb{E}[\sum_{i = 1}^n X_{i - 1} \Delta W_i] = \sum_{i = 1} \mathbb{E}[X_{i - 1}] \mathbb{E}[\Delta W_i] = 0 \]

Then, as \(n \to \infty\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0\) for all \(t > 0\).

So,

\[ \mathbb{E}[\int_0^t W_s dW_s] = \mathbb{E} [\frac{1}{2} W_t^2 - \frac{1}{2} t] \] \[ = 0 \]

The expectation of \(W_t^2\) is just the variance of \(W_t\) which is normally distributed as \(mathcal{N}(0, t)\). So the \(\frac{1}{2} t\) "has to" exist to produce an expectation of \(0\).

docs.title: The Heart
docs.text:
We observe that \(\text{l.i.m} \sum_{i = 1}^n \Delta W_i^2 = t\). So we can write this as:

\[ \int_0^t dW_s^2 = t \]

By applying FTC, we recover \(dW_t^2 = dt\). This cannot be taken literally - squared increment of Brownian motion does not equal to time increment.

docs.title: \(dW_t^2 = dt\)
docs.text:
Suppose \(\mathbb{E}[G_s^2] < M\) for all \(s \in [t_0, t]\) for some constant \(M > 0\). Then, we have:

\[ \int_{t_0}^t G_s dW_s^2 := \text{l.i.m.} \sum_{i = 1}^n G_{i - 1} \Delta W_i^2 \]

Theorem: This mean-square limits is equal to \(\int_{t_0}^t G_s ds\) where \(ds\) is an ordinary differential.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Consider a time-interval sliced \(0 \leq t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n = T\).

\[ \int_0^T G_s ds \approx \sum_i G_{t_i} (t_{i + 1} - t_i) = \sum_i G_{t_i} \Delta t \] \[ \int_0^T G_s dW_s^2 \approx \sum_i G_{t_i} (W_{t_{i + 1}} - W_{t_i}) = \sum_i G_{t_i} \Delta W_i^2 \]

On a single slice, \(\Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t)\). Each random increment has mean square \(\Delta t\): \(\mathbb{E}[\Delta W_i^2] = \Delta t\). Each \(\Delta W_i^2\) is not exactly \(\Delta t\) but if you sum them, the sum's variance becomes linear in \(\Delta t\) and goes to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\).

It's like using statistically regular movements as a clock. Suppose we have a rat which runs at a reliable rate (it will move as \(\Delta W \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t)\) over \(\Delta t\) seconds). To use this rat as a clock, we can measure its movements at a really fine scale and square the movement to get a positive quantity. Each squared step follows a \(\Delta t \cdot \chi^2(1)\) distribution with expectation \(\Delta t\) and variance \(2 \Delta t^2\) - the square distance the rat moves is like a noisy estimator of how much time has passed. Fine scale measurement gives so many estimates that the LLN averages out the noise and in the limit, we get a reliable measurement of total time \(T\).

docs.title: CCA
docs.text:
Canonical Correlation Analysis is dimensionality reduction - similar to PCA but it simulatenously reduces the dimensions of two random vectors (or datasets) \(X, Y\). Instead of trying to maximize variance explained (PCA objective), it tries to maximize \(\text{Corr}(X, Y)\).

Let \(X \in \R^{n \times d_x}, Y \in \R^{n \times d_y}\). Here, \(n\) is the number of data-points.

Let \(k \leq \min(d_x, d_y, n)\) and \(A, B\) be sketching matrices, \(A \in \R^{d_x \times k}, B \in \R^{d_y \times k}\). \(k\) is the target dimension.

Let \(XA = z_x \in \R^{n \times k}, YB = z_y \in \R^{n \times k}\).

CCA solves the following optimization problem:

\[ \max_{A, B} \text{Tr}(\frac{1}{n} z_x^T z_y) \]

such that \(\frac{1}{n} z_x^T z_k = \frac{1}{n} z_y^T z_y = I\).

In other words, maximize the trace of the cross-correlation matrix between embeddings such that embeddings have unit variance and zero covariance.

In PCA, there is a connection between maximizing variance and minimizing prediction error. Similarly, there's a relationship between cross-correlation trace and embedding prediction error.

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n ||z_x^{(i)} - z_y^{(i)}||^2 = \frac{1}{n} ||z_x - z_y||_F^2 \]

The Frobenius norm of a matrix essentially flattens a matrix into a long vector and finds its standard Euclidean norm. The above equality holds b/c we're takiing the MSE over all data-points between the sketched matrices - which is the same as if we were to flatten the two matrices and take their Frobenius norm.

NOTE - why?

Then, we have:

\[ = \frac{1}{n} \left ( \text{Tr}(z_x^T z_x) + \text{Tr}(z_y^T z_y) - 2 \text{Tr}(z_x^T z_y) \right ) \]

Due to the above constraints, we know that each individual embedding matrix's covariance is \(I\). So we have:

\[ = \frac{2k}{n} - \frac{2}{n} \text{Tr}(z_x^T z_y) \]

Therefore, we can write CCA as:

\[ \min_{A, B} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n ||z_x^{(i)} - z_y^{(i)}||^2 \]

with unit embedding covariances \(\frac{1}{n} z_x^T z_x = \frac{1}{n} z_y^T z_y = I\).

JEPA is similar to CCA but non-linear and without dimensional constraints (due to the non-linearity) which can result in representational collapse. Techniques like SIGReg are attempts to build in whitening constraints into the induced embeddings from a learned encoder.

docs.title: Understanding Typicality
docs.text:
• Understanding Typicality
  • Blog Review
    • Coins
    • Gaussians
    • Typicality
    • Paradoxes
      • Language
      • OOD detection
    • Conclusion
      • Citations

I have previously come across typicality in a couple of contexts

  • In using MCMC estimators in high dimensions, an integral tends to concentrate its \(\text{volume} * \text{density}\) on a thin surface called the typical set where the Markov Chain should ideally spend most of its time. High dimensional Gaussians are frequently analogized to soap bubbles (I think of them like pound cakes). The density is concentrated around the distribution's mode but there is also very little volume around the mode. The typical set is thus like a film around the mode where both the probability density and the volume are non-negligible (hence where most of the integral is).

  • The AEP (Asymptotic Equipartition Property) in information theory states that there is a set of sequences called the typical set where as the length of the sequence grows, the probability of this set approaches \(1\). Additionally, the distribution over this set is roughly uniform and the single most likely sequence is frequently not in this set.

For the first point, much of my intuition comes from this paper and talk by Michael Betancourt.

docs.title: Blog Review
docs.text: Maximum likelihood training is simple and intuitive. However, for generative models, higher likelihoods frequently do not correlate to visual fidelity and can produce very unintuitive results. This post excludes overfitting as a possible explainer as that is not unique to likelihood based models.

docs.title: Coins
docs.text:
Consider the binomial distribution \(B(n, p)\) where \(n = 16, p = \frac{3}{4}\) modeling a sequence of biased coin flips. On average, we would expect to see about \(12\) heads and \(4\) tails with some room for error. Here, we are treating sequences as unordered sets.

Let \(Y\) be the sequence \((x_1, \dots, x_{16})\). What is \(\text{argmax}_Y \ P(Y)\), the single most likely sequence?

The single most likely sequence is all heads. The probability of this sequence is \((\frac{3}{4})^{16} = 0.01\). While this sequence is the single most likely sequence, we would be shocked if we actually ended up counting \(16\) heads as that would mean not a single coin landed on tails.

On the contrary, let \(X\) be the number of heads observed. The most likely number of heads to be observed is \(12\). The specific probability of observing \(12\) heads is \(C(16, 4) * (\frac{3}{4})^{12} (\frac{1}{4})^4\). While each individual sequence containing \(12\) heads is not as likely as the sequence with \(16\) heads, there are \(C(16, 4)\) ways to get \(12\) heads while there is only one way to get \(16\) heads.

docs.title: Gaussians
docs.text:
Gaussian Densities can be analogized to soap bubbles... or pound cakes!

As was stated earlier, high-dimensional Gaussians concentrate their probability density around the mode. However, computing an integral involves multiplying this density against \(dx\), a little piece of volume. In high-dimensional spaces, there is more volume further away from any given point. There is simply more space for the distribution to exist over further away from the mode (at the peak of the pound cake / surface of the soap bubble). This is the continuous version of the coin example - \(16\) heads is the single most likely sequence but there are more ways to get \(12\) heads. Similarly, if you had a hundred-dimensional Gaussian centered around \(\vec{0}\), you would still be extremely surprised to observe \(\vec{0}\) as a sample.

This is stated formally in many textbooks as the Gaussian annulus theorem.

docs.title: Typicality
docs.text:
Entropy can be written as

\[ H(X) = \mathbb{E}_{X \sim p} \left [ \log \frac{1}{p(X)} \right ] \]

Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are i.i.d. \(\sim p\). If \(H(X) < \infty\), then by LLN

\[ \frac{1}{n} \log \frac{1}{p(X_1, \dots, X_n)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n \log \frac{1}{p(X_i)} \to_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\log \frac{1}{p(X)}] = H(X) \]

Then, for \(\epsilon > 0\), define the typical set

\[ \mathcal{T}_{n}^{\epsilon} = \{x^n \in \mathcal{X}^n: p(x^n) \in [2^{-n(H(X) + \epsilon)}, 2^{-n(H(X) - \epsilon)}] \} \]

Each sequence in the typical set carries roughly as much information as expected (within \(\epsilon\) of the distribution's entropy). To see this, simply reverse:

\[ \frac{1}{n} \log \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{x})} \approx H(X) \] \[ \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{x})} \approx 2^{n H(X)} \] \[ p(\mathbf{x}) \approx 2^{- n H(X)} \]

The negative log likelihood of each of these sequences is close to the distribution's entropy. As the dimensionality increases, the probability that each random sample drawn from the distribution is part of a given typical set \(\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\) approaches \(1\). Random samples will nearly always be 'typical' and the typical set covers most of the distribution's support.

Additionally, like mentioned earlier (and illustrated with the coin example), the mode frequently is not part of the typical set. Individual samples with exceptional likelihoods are in fact atypical and we shouldn't expect to observe them during sampling.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: In autoregressive models + beam search, we sometimes may want to find the single most likely sentence ('MAP decoding') or something akin to that. However, those familiar with language models know that in setting temperature to \(0\), we get degenerate or repetitive sentences. This repetitivity is atypical but has high likelihoods precisely because it is more predictable.

docs.title: OOD detection
docs.text: OOD detection asks if an input plausibly could have been drawn from some distribution. Typically, we assume that OOD inputs have low-likelihoods and in-distribution inputs have high-likelihoods (we are likely to sample them). However, the mode of a distribution has a very high likelihood but as we established, we are extremely unlikely to sample the mode as it is not part of the typical set.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
It may be preferable to learn fidelity using 'intuitive' likelihood or to learn some kind of perceptual metric.

After reading this blog, I feel that I have a much better handle on typicality and its relationship with likelihoods. I believe the first intuition which is that in high-dimensional spaces, volume grows the further we move from a given spot, explains this phenomenon of Gaussian "soap bubbles". The trap of examining atypically likely samples (like the mode) seems to be the clearest connection between typicality and machine learning.
